title: High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution Via Full Core-mode Encoding Over Deployed Multicore Fibers
authors: G. H. Dos Santos, K. B. Sawada, N. Villalba, C. Jara, N. Guerrero, C. Melo, M. H. Magiotto, D. Mart\'inez, G. B. Xavier, J. Cari\~ne, G. Saavedra, E. S. G\'omez, S. P. Walborn, G. Lima
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security rooted in quantum physics, while high-dimensional (HD) encoding increases both noise tolerance and secret-key yield. Multicore fibers (MCFs), a leading platform for next-generation telecom networks, are a natural substrate for HD-QKD. Field demonstrations over deployed MCFs have so far relied on a hybrid qudit encoding strategy that combines two path (core modes) with the time-bin photonic degree of freedom, rather than exploiting the full set of available core modes. Although practical, this approach incurs intrinsic efficiency penalties that grow with dimension. Here we implement a four-dimensional ([MATH]) QKD protocol that directly exploits the full set of core modes of a four-core MCF, operating over an installed MCF network across the Universidad de Concepci\'on campus under continuous environmental perturbations. We further benchmark the scheme using superconducting nanowire detectors at [MATH]dB channel loss, achieving a composable finite-key rate of [MATH]bits/pulse, the highest per-pulse rate reported to date for HD-QKD at comparable loss. This result establishes core-mode encoding as a viable architecture for realistic, high-rate quantum-secure communications.
tldr: Demonstrates high-dimensional QKD using all core modes of a deployed four-core multicore fiber, achieving record per-pulse secret-key rates.
motivation: Previous HD-QKD over MCFs used hybrid encoding (core modes + time-bin) with efficiency penalties; this work aims to exploit the full set of core modes for higher efficiency and rate.
method: Implements a 4-dimensional QKD protocol using all four core modes of a deployed MCF, with superconducting nanowire detectors, under real environmental perturbations.
result: Achieves a composable finite-key rate of 0.22 bits/pulse at 8 dB channel loss, the highest per-pulse rate reported for HD-QKD at comparable loss.
conclusion: Core-mode encoding is a viable architecture for high-rate quantum-secure communications over installed MCF networks, with potential for scaling to higher dimensions.

title: Characterization Of Errors In Photon-heralded Quantum Operations Between Non-interacting Quantum Emitters
authors: Mahsa Karimi, Samuel Mister, Christoph Simon, Stephen C. Wein
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an analytic perturbative framework that enables the analysis of small Markovian errors in probabilistic, photon-heralded quantum operations between non-interacting emitters. Building on and extending the Zero-Photon-Generation (ZPG) framework, we derive closed-form perturbative solutions that capture both ideal (zero-order) and noisy (low-order) gate dynamics conditioned on time-integrated photon counting. Our framework provides analytic solutions to process matrices and Pauli error weights up to leading order, bridging the gap between detailed physical imperfections of a system and its corresponding abstract Pauli noise models. Moreover, our framework captures imperfections across the full physical system stack, from photon generation to optical manipulation. We benchmark the resulting perturbative predictions on a repeat-until-success CZ gate against numerical simulations, demonstrating accurate modeling of source-induced noise, and then apply the same framework to analyze coherent phase-shifter miscalibrations as a representative example of optical-manipulation errors. The methods developed in this work enable physics-informed parameter tuning to optimize gate designs and develop tailored quantum error correction protocols toward fault-tolerant quantum computing using hybrid light--matter quantum systems.
tldr: Develops an analytic perturbative framework for modeling Markovian errors in photon-heralded quantum operations between non-interacting emitters, bridging physical imperfections to Pauli noise models.
motivation: To enable accurate modeling of noise in hybrid light-matter quantum systems for fault-tolerant quantum computing, where photon-heralded gates are promising but suffer from various physical imperfections.
method: Extends the Zero-Photon-Generation (ZPG) framework with closed-form perturbative solutions up to leading order, capturing errors from photon generation to optical manipulation, and benchmarks against numerical simulations.
result: Provides analytic process matrices and Pauli error weights for a repeat-until-success CZ gate, accurately modeling source-induced noise and optical miscalibrations.
conclusion: Enables physics-informed parameter tuning and tailored quantum error correction protocols for hybrid quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum repeaters and networks.

title: Anisotropic Rabi Model As A Noise Biased Qubit
authors: Jia-Wen Yu, Ke-Xiong Yan, Yuan Qiu, Yiming Yu, Yexiong Zeng, Adam Miranowicz, Zhi-Cheng Shi, Ye-Hong Chen, Yan Xia, Franco Nori
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the quantum anisotropic Rabi model as a potential resource for a noise biased qubit. The system-environment coupling can be biased by tuning the relative strengths of the rotating-wave and counter-rotating-wave interactions, characterized by the anisotropy parameter [MATH]. This anisotropy selectively suppresses dominant decoherence pathways, thereby enabling the construction of a protected logical qubit in the ultrastrong and deep-strong coupling regimes. The logical states (formed by the ground and first excited states of the anisotropic Rabi model) possess coherence times that are enhanced compared to the isotropic case. Moreover, we construct a set of universal gate operations within the logical-state subspace and demonstrate that the gate operations associated with different values of [MATH] exhibit robustness against external noise. These findings are expected to inspire applications and research directions for the anisotropic Rabi model with promising potential impacts.
tldr: The anisotropic Rabi model is proposed as a noise-biased qubit with enhanced coherence and robust gate operations in the ultrastrong and deep-strong coupling regimes.
motivation: To overcome decoherence in superconducting qubits by exploiting the anisotropic Rabi model's ability to suppress dominant noise channels via tuning rotating-wave and counter-rotating-wave interactions.
method: Theoretical analysis of the anisotropic Rabi model's energy levels and decoherence properties, with logical qubit encoding in the ground and first excited states; universal gate operations are constructed within the logical subspace.
result: The anisotropic Rabi model yields a noise-biased qubit with coherence times enhanced over the isotropic case, and gate operations show robustness against external noise.
conclusion: The findings suggest the anisotropic Rabi model is a promising platform for protected qubits and may inspire further research in quantum computing with ultrastrong coupling.

title: Arbitrary Manipulation Of Nuclear Spins In Hexagonal Boron Nitride
authors: Mehdi Abdi Fattah Sakuldee
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to its localized nature and controllability, the negatively charged boron vacancy centers (V[MATH]) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are a promising spin platform for accessing its neighboring nuclei with potential for performing quantum computational tasks. However, the methods of utilizing and manipulating the nuclear spins are still lacking. In this work, we propose a protocol for the preparation of single- and multi-qubit gates on the nuclear spins, utilizing the electron spin as an auxiliary qubit. By applying a background magnetic field and a multi-tone continuous drive, we show that the electron spin coupling to the nuclei can be efficiently engineered. This allows for suppressing the undesired electron-nuclear interactions through the Hahn echo pulse sequence. The target gates are then implemented by employing proper RF drives. Our numerical results for realistic parameters show gate fidelities as high as [MATH] for single-qubit and [MATH] for multi-qubit gates. With the gate execution durations being less than [MATH] ns, our protocol evades electron spin decoherence effects. Therefore, our scheme sets the stage for the practical application of V[MATH] in hBN for quantum computation purposes.
tldr: Proposes a protocol using electron spin as auxiliary to manipulate nuclear spins in hBN for quantum gates.
motivation: To enable quantum computation using nuclear spins in hBN, which lack manipulation methods despite promising spin properties.
method: Applies background magnetic field and multi-tone continuous drive to engineer electron-nuclear coupling, suppresses unwanted interactions via Hahn echo, and implements gates with RF drives.
result: Achieves high-fidelity single- and multi-qubit gates (up to ~99%) with durations under 100 ns, avoiding electron spin decoherence.
conclusion: Sets stage for practical quantum computation using V_B^- centers in hBN, with potential for scalable quantum networks.

title: Distributed Variational Quantum Optimisation By Entanglement-Selective Transport
authors: Edric Matwiejew, Pascal Elahi, Ugo Varetto
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum optimisation is challenging because computing the problem cost function across multiple quantum processors requires non-local gates, which can incur overhead in latency and fidelity. Here we introduce QESTO, a distributed variational ansatz for graph-based discrete optimisation that requires only persistent pre-shared Bell pairs for remote operations. Using local operations, it encodes local constraint information in the Bell pairs that is leveraged to produce amplitude transfer towards globally valid distributed solution states. QESTO requires one Bell pair per distributed edge of the problem graph and, after initialisation of the Bell states, uses no non-local gates. On two bounded weighted Wang tile-matching problem ensembles, QESTO achieves stronger convergence to low-cost tilings than equivalently partitioned QAOA with no distributed gates at ansatz depths of two or higher, and exceeds the mean performance of monolithic QAOA at the deepest studied depth in both ensembles. These results suggest that persistent entanglement can support useful variational communication while reducing per-layer non-local gate overhead.
tldr: QESTO uses pre-shared Bell pairs to enable distributed variational quantum optimization without non-local gates, achieving better convergence than partitioned QAOA on tiling problems.
motivation: Distributed quantum optimization faces overhead from non-local gates; the authors aim to reduce this overhead by using persistent entanglement for communication.
method: They propose a variational ansatz that encodes local constraint information into pre-shared Bell pairs via local operations, enabling amplitude transfer toward valid distributed solutions without non-local gates.
result: On two bounded weighted Wang tile-matching ensembles, QESTO outperforms equivalently partitioned QAOA at depths ≥2 and exceeds monolithic QAOA at the deepest depth studied.
conclusion: Persistent entanglement can serve as a resource for variational communication, reducing per-layer non-local gate overhead and suggesting new directions for distributed quantum computing.

title: An Effective Pauli-Channel Model For Passive-User Loop-Back Qkd
authors: Luis Adri\'an Lizama-P\'erez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work develops an effective channel model for distributed passive-user Loop-Back quantum key distribution. In the intended key-establishment setting, the two passive users \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) are the legitimate lightweight parties that establish a shared secret key by using Alice as an active quantum preparation-and-measurement infrastructure. A single active station prepares and measures BB84 states, while two remote users apply only local polarization rotations. We show that the passive-user pair can be externally encapsulated as an effective Loop-Back node whose observable action is a balanced mixture of conjugate-basis dephasings, equivalently represented as an anisotropic Pauli channel with identity, \(X\), and \(Z\) components and no \(Y\) component. This structure differs from isotropic depolarization and recovers the ideal conclusive-event probability \(P_{}=1/4\). The model also clarifies why non-orthogonal intermediate states are necessary for passive-user security. This channel-level description characterizes Alice's observable statistics and provides a compact basis for subsequent analysis of passive-user Loop-Back QKD under realistic optical and adversarial conditions.
tldr: This paper models passive-user Loop-Back QKD as an effective Pauli channel with identity, X, and Z components, showing that the channel is anisotropic and recovers ideal conclusive-event probability.
motivation: To provide a compact channel-level description for passive-user Loop-Back QKD, which is a variant of QKD where two passive users share a key via an active station, and to clarify the necessity of non-orthogonal intermediate states for security.
method: The authors encapsulate the two passive users and the active station as an effective Loop-Back node, deriving that the observable action is a balanced mixture of conjugate-basis dephasings, equivalent to an anisotropic Pauli channel with no Y component.
result: The effective channel is an anisotropic Pauli channel with identity, X, and Z components, differing from isotropic depolarization, and the ideal conclusive-event probability is 1/4. The model explains why non-orthogonal intermediate states are needed for security.
conclusion: This channel model provides a compact basis for analyzing passive-user Loop-Back QKD under realistic conditions, including optical and adversarial scenarios, and may inform the design of practical QKD systems with passive users.

title: Continuous-Variable Quantum State Tomography Enabled By Quantum Mirrors
authors: Mariano Uria, Amaru Moya, Carla Hermann-Avigliano, Pablo Solano, Aldo Delgado
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum technologies, continuous-variable systems offer advantages over their discrete counterparts. However, continuous-variable tomography suffers from exponentially growing sample complexity. We propose protocols using quantum mirrors to transfer the complete information of incident photonic states onto a control atomic system. This enables full photonic state characterization through measurements on the control atom alone, realized via kernel functions, direct wavefunction reconstruction, and pointwise Wigner function measurements. Our approach overcomes the limitations of conventional photon counting, statistical inference, and inverse transformation, providing a robust framework for benchmarking and verifying non-Gaussian states in continuous-variable quantum optics.
tldr: Proposes quantum mirror protocols to transfer continuous-variable photonic state information to a control atom, enabling full tomography via atomic measurements and overcoming sample complexity.
motivation: Continuous-variable quantum state tomography suffers from exponentially growing sample complexity, limiting characterization of non-Gaussian states.
method: Uses quantum mirrors to map photonic states onto a control atomic system, then performs tomography via kernel functions, direct wavefunction reconstruction, and pointwise Wigner function measurements on the atom.
result: The approach bypasses conventional photon counting and statistical inference, providing a robust framework for benchmarking non-Gaussian states.
conclusion: Enables efficient continuous-variable tomography with potential applications in quantum communication and computing, though experimental realization remains challenging.

title: Robust Steerability Classification Via Key Feature Extraction And Matrix Structure Preservation
authors: Yutao Xin, Huixian Meng, Zhongyan Li, Pu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalization ability is essential for assessing the robustness of quantum steerability classifiers. In this work, we investigate robust steerability classification from the perspective of key feature extraction and matrix structure preservation. The dataset introduced in Phys. Rev. A 100, 022314 (2019) provides the training basis for the present work. With strictly unsteerable random states, T-diagonal states, and All-Versus-Nothing (AVN) states, we evaluate the generalization performance of support vector machines (SVMs), multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), and deep perceptron control classifiers(DPs) trained on full-information features. None of these classifiers perform consistently on T-diagonal or AVN states. Given that stochastic local operations and classical communication and local unitary transformations preserve steerability, we introduce a key feature that determines steerability. SVMs trained on this feature overcome the instability on T-diagonal states but still fail on AVN states. Moreover, this feature alone is insufficient for training robust neural-network-based steerability classifiers. Recognizing that flattening quantum states into one-dimensional vectors may destroy their intrinsic matrix structure, we introduce matrix versions of both features and train convolutional neural networks on them. The most robust overall performance among the tested classifiers is achieved only when the matrix structure is preserved and key features are extracted simultaneously. Finally, as an application, we employ the most robust classifiers to predict the number of projective measurements required to detect the steerability of axially symmetric states.
tldr: This paper investigates robust steerability classification by extracting key features and preserving matrix structure, achieving improved generalization across different state classes.
motivation: Existing steerability classifiers fail to generalize across different types of quantum states (T-diagonal, AVN). The authors aim to develop robust classifiers by leveraging steerability-preserving operations and matrix structure.
method: They train SVMs, MLPs, and deep perceptron classifiers on full-information features, then introduce a key feature derived from stochastic local operations and classical communication (SLOCC) and local unitary transformations. They also propose matrix versions of features to preserve the intrinsic matrix structure and train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on them.
result: SVMs trained on the key feature overcome instability on T-diagonal states but fail on AVN states. Only when both key features and matrix structure are preserved (using CNNs) do classifiers achieve robust performance across all state classes.
conclusion: Preserving matrix structure and extracting key features simultaneously is crucial for robust steerability classification. The most robust classifiers are applied to predict the number of projective measurements needed to detect steerability of axially symmetric states.

title: Leggett-Garg Test Inequality With Spin And Flavour Neutrino Oscillations In A Constant Magnetic Field
authors: S. D. Madrid I. A. Monroy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Leggett-Garg inequality (LGI), an analogue of Bell\'s inequality involving correlations of measurements of one observable on a system at different times, stands as one of the hallmark tests of quantum mechanics against classical predictions. In this work, we investigate its implications in the context of neutrino flavour ([MATH]) and spin ([MATH]) oscillations in the presence of a constant transverse magnetic field. For systems with strong magnetic fields, we show that, for both cases, there are length regions [MATH] where the LGI is violated, as quantified by the correlator functions [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: This paper tests Leggett-Garg inequality violations in neutrino flavor and spin oscillations under a constant magnetic field, finding regions where quantum mechanics defies classical realism.
motivation: To extend tests of quantumness (Leggett-Garg inequality) to neutrino systems, which are fundamental particles, and to explore the effect of magnetic fields on such tests.
method: The authors compute the Leggett-Garg correlator functions for neutrino flavor and spin oscillations in the presence of a constant transverse magnetic field, analyzing the parameter space for violations.
result: For both flavor and spin oscillations, there exist length regions where the Leggett-Garg inequality is violated, indicating nonclassical behavior.
conclusion: Neutrino oscillations provide a new arena for testing quantum foundations, and magnetic fields can influence the violation, suggesting potential applications in probing quantum coherence in neutrino systems.

title: Magnetic Field Free Nonreciprocity In Tapered Atomic Cladded Nano Waveguide
authors: Ilan Sher (the Hebrew University Of Jerusalem, Israel), Benyamin Shnirman (university Of Stuttgart, Germany, Institut F\"ur Mikroelektronik Stuttgart, Germany), Arieh Grosman (the Hebrew University Of Jerusalem, Israel), Roy Zektzer (bar-Ilan University, Israel), Markus Greul (institut F\"ur Mikroelektronik Stuttgart, Germany), Mathias Kaschel (institut F\"ur Mikroelektronik Stuttgart, Germany), Tilman Pfau (university Of Stuttgart, Germany), Robert L\"ow (university Of Stuttgart, Germany), Uriel Levy
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical nonreciprocity is a fundamental requirement for modern optical communications and quantum information processing, where it is essential to protect sensitive sources from destabilizing feedback and preserving quantum coherence. Conventional nonreciprocal devices are based on the Faraday effect; however, their dependence on bulky permanent magnets poses a significant barrier to chip-scale integration and scalability. Moreover, the application of a magnetic field is undesired in many quantum atomic systems. In this work, we demonstrate magnet-free optical nonreciprocity on a fully integrated platform utilizing a Nanophotonic Alkali Silicon Waveguide (NASWAG) interfaced with hot rubidium vapor. By employing velocity-selective optical pumping (VSOP), we break time reversal symmetry by taking advantage of the Doppler effect-generated by the thermally moving atoms, a phenomenon traditionally viewed as a limitation in atomic spectroscopy. We show that the use of suspended tapered waveguides significantly mitigates transit-time broadening, thereby enabling the observation of a robust nonreciprocal response. We further characterize the dependence of the isolation contrast on pump power, finding that the experimental measurements and numerical simulations correspond and provide mutual support for the underlying physical model. With proper optimization, the demonstrated effect may be used in the future for applications such as magnetic free optical isolators.
tldr: Demonstrates magnet-free optical nonreciprocity in a nanophotonic waveguide integrated with hot atomic vapor using velocity-selective optical pumping.
motivation: To achieve chip-scale optical isolation without magnetic fields, which is crucial for quantum information processing and integrated photonics.
method: A suspended tapered nanophotonic waveguide (NASWAG) is interfaced with hot rubidium vapor; velocity-selective optical pumping breaks time-reversal symmetry via the Doppler effect, enabling nonreciprocal transmission.
result: Robust nonreciprocal response observed with isolation contrast depending on pump power; experimental results match numerical simulations.
conclusion: The approach offers a path to magnetic-free optical isolators on chip, potentially benefiting quantum communication and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Nonreciprocal Dispersive Coupling For Quantum Sensing
authors: Chunling Xu Dong Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dispersive coupling is widely utilized for quantum information readout. Most prior studies have concentrated on reciprocal dispersive coupling. Here, we further construct nonreciprocal dispersive coupling and apply it to quantum sensing. For cavity photon number measurement, nonreciprocal dispersive coupling delivers higher precision than its reciprocal counterpart, and this advantage grows more pronounced with an increase in photon number. When directly measuring the single-photon driving strength, however, nonreciprocal dispersive coupling shows no superiority over reciprocal dispersive coupling. By converting the information of driving strength into cavity photon numbers via our proposed strategy, nonreciprocal dispersive coupling again outperforms reciprocal dispersive coupling in precision, with the advantage becoming increasingly significant at larger driving strength. This work presents a novel method to boost quantum sensing and enable the fabrication of ultra-precise quantum sensors.
tldr: This paper introduces nonreciprocal dispersive coupling and demonstrates its advantage over reciprocal coupling for quantum sensing, particularly in cavity photon number measurement.
motivation: Dispersive coupling is widely used for quantum information readout, but most studies focus on reciprocal coupling. The authors aim to explore nonreciprocal dispersive coupling to enhance quantum sensing precision.
method: The authors theoretically construct a nonreciprocal dispersive coupling scheme and analyze its performance for measuring cavity photon number and single-photon driving strength, comparing it to reciprocal coupling.
result: Nonreciprocal dispersive coupling yields higher precision for cavity photon number measurement, with the advantage increasing with photon number. For direct driving strength measurement, no advantage is observed, but by converting driving strength information into photon numbers, nonreciprocal coupling again outperforms reciprocal coupling.
conclusion: This work provides a novel method to boost quantum sensing precision, potentially enabling ultra-precise quantum sensors, and suggests further exploration of nonreciprocal effects in quantum metrology.

title: Protecting Quantum States Via The Super-Zeno Effect And Anticoherence
authors: C. Chryssomalakos, A. G. Flores-Delgado, E. Guzm\'an-Gonz\'alez, L. Hanotel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a spin system coupled to a noisy environment via an interaction Hamiltonian [MATH] which is a polynomial of degree [MATH] in the spin operators [MATH] ([MATH]-magnetic Hamiltonian), and show that the use of the quantum super-Zeno effect in conjunction with a spin-anticoherent subspace, is highly effective in protecting the spin from the noise. When [MATH], as in the case of unwanted rotations induced by stray magnetic fields, our scheme provides a quantum gyroscope, a concept that generalizes naturally to higher [MATH] values (a quantum [MATH]-gyroscope). The gist of the proposed protocol is to use the quantum super-Zeno effect to confine a state to the subspace, and then exploit anticoherence to freeze its evolution within it.
tldr: The paper proposes using the quantum super-Zeno effect combined with spin-anticoherent subspaces to protect quantum states from noise, generalizing to a quantum gyroscope concept.
motivation: To develop a method for protecting quantum states from environmental noise, particularly unwanted rotations from stray magnetic fields, which is crucial for quantum information processing.
method: The authors consider a spin system coupled to a noisy environment via a polynomial interaction Hamiltonian. They apply the quantum super-Zeno effect to confine the state to a subspace and then use anticoherence to freeze its evolution within that subspace.
result: The combination of super-Zeno and anticoherence is highly effective in protecting the spin from noise, and for linear noise (k=1) it provides a quantum gyroscope, generalizable to higher k as a quantum k-gyroscope.
conclusion: The protocol offers a novel way to protect quantum states, with potential applications in quantum sensing and metrology, and opens avenues for further exploration of anticoherence in noise protection.

title: Quantum Error Correction With The Toric Code
authors: Collaborators Atom Computing
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing platforms based on arrays of tweezer-confined neutral atoms have recently emerged as a competitive modality thanks to a direct path toward high qubit count, rapidly advancing operation fidelities, and their ability to execute circuits with arbitrary qubit connectivity. These features will enable the use of efficient error correction schemes with high encoding-rates, time-efficient decoding, and resource-efficient architectures based on transversal gates. With these goals in mind, recent state of the art neutral atom demonstrations focus on the transition from the use of physical qubits to error-corrected logical qubits, but to date there has been no demonstration of repeated error correction scalable to arbitrary depth. Here, we demonstrate many cycles of syndrome extraction in a toric quantum error correcting code, using mid-circuit measurement and replacement of lost qubits, including reloading of a qubit reservoir for indefinite coherent operation. We characterize the logical error rate after up to 90 cycles, showing that logical information can be preserved through multiple rounds of qubit reloading. Comparing two distances of the code up to 8 rounds of syndrome extraction shows a lower absolute logical error rate for the larger distance code.
tldr: Demonstration of repeated syndrome extraction and qubit reloading in a toric code using neutral atom arrays, enabling scalable error correction.
motivation: To achieve fault-tolerant quantum computation, scalable error correction with high encoding rates and resource-efficient architectures is needed. Neutral atom platforms offer arbitrary connectivity and high qubit counts, but repeated error correction to arbitrary depth had not been demonstrated.
method: Implemented a toric quantum error correcting code on a neutral atom array with mid-circuit measurement, qubit reloading from a reservoir, and multiple cycles of syndrome extraction.
result: Demonstrated up to 90 cycles of syndrome extraction with logical error rates characterized; larger distance code showed lower logical error rate over 8 rounds.
conclusion: The work shows that neutral atom platforms can support repeated error correction with qubit reloading, paving the way for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Quantum Simulations Of Ultrafast Optical Spectroscopy Of Semiconductors On Digital Quantum Computers In The Semi-classical Approximation
authors: Mykhailo Klymenko, Bahar Goldozian, Thong Hoang, Jared H. Cole, Muhammad Usman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a digital quantum simulation framework for ultrafast optical spectroscopy of semiconductor materials. The framework is based on Brillouin-zone discretization and the second-quantization formalism, and is designed as a quantum alternative to classical simulations based on the semiconductor Bloch equations. Its current capabilities include quantum simulations of linear absorption and optical gain spectra, incorporating Lorentzian broadening, finite-temperature band-filling effects, and reduced-dimensionality effects. Benchmark comparisons with classical simulations for GaAs demonstrate quantitative agreement in the noiseless limit. The inclusion of realistic hardware noise of NISQ-era quantum computers effectively manifests itself as an additional source of scattering processes, resulting in increased spectral broadening. While no exponential quantum advantage is expected in the single-particle approximation, the framework naturally extends to many-body regimes where classical simulations face the hierarchy problem and exponential scaling and provable quantum advantage will be possible. The quantum simulations considered in this work capture central elements of semiconductor spectroscopy, the aspects such as open quantum systems, light-matter interactions, statistical mechanics, non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, and many-body physics. As such, it provides a physically motivated and scalable model for benchmarking quantum computers in applications to complex, real-world problems.
tldr: This paper presents a digital quantum simulation framework for ultrafast optical spectroscopy of semiconductors, using Brillouin-zone discretization and second quantization, with benchmark results on GaAs.
motivation: Classical simulations of semiconductor spectroscopy face challenges in many-body regimes due to exponential scaling; quantum computers may offer advantages for such problems.
method: The framework discretizes the Brillouin zone and uses second-quantization formalism to simulate linear absorption and optical gain spectra on digital quantum computers, incorporating Lorentzian broadening, finite-temperature effects, and reduced dimensionality.
result: Benchmark comparisons with classical simulations for GaAs show quantitative agreement in the noiseless limit; realistic hardware noise introduces additional spectral broadening.
conclusion: While no exponential quantum advantage is expected in the single-particle approximation, the framework extends to many-body regimes where classical methods struggle, providing a scalable model for benchmarking quantum computers.

title: Quantification Of Entanglement In Three-Qubit Systems
authors: Zikra Aram
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents an analytical investigation of entanglement quantification in three-qubit pure states through the Ac\'in canonical representation, which serves as a generalization of the two-qubit Schmidt decomposition. Driven by the intricacies of multipartite entanglement and the shortcomings of current measures, we employ a global concurrence measure derived from the generalized concurrence of various bipartitions within the system. The characteristics of this measure are explored both analytically and numerically across a range of SLOCC entanglement classes, such as product, biseparable, GHZ-type, and W-type states. When compared to the three-tangle and tripartite negativity, our findings indicate that this measure yields complementary insights into multipartite correlations. The outcomes underscore the significance of this measure in elucidating the structure and distribution of entanglement within three-qubit quantum systems.
tldr: This paper quantifies entanglement in three-qubit pure states using a global concurrence measure based on bipartitions, comparing it to the three-tangle and tripartite negativity.
motivation: Multipartite entanglement is complex and existing measures have shortcomings; a more comprehensive quantification is needed.
method: The authors use the Acín canonical representation to parametrize three-qubit states and define a global concurrence from generalized concurrences of all bipartitions, analyzing it analytically and numerically across SLOCC classes.
result: The global concurrence provides complementary insights to the three-tangle and tripartite negativity, effectively distinguishing different entanglement classes.
conclusion: This measure helps elucidate the structure and distribution of entanglement in three-qubit systems, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Comment On "Possibility Of Superradiant Neutrino Emission By Atomic Condensate" By M. Blasone, L. Gastaldo And F. Romeo, Phys. Rev. D 113, 053010 (2026)
authors: Wolfgang Ketterle, Hanzhen Lin, Yu-Kun Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the recent proposal for superradiant emission of neutrinos cannot evade our proof that superradiant neutrino emission is fundamentally impossible. Pairing two fermions in a molecule does not remove the cancellation of interference terms in neutrino emission due to fermionic anticommutators.
tldr: This comment refutes a proposal for superradiant neutrino emission from atomic condensates, arguing that fermionic anticommutators fundamentally prevent such emission.
motivation: To correct a recent claim that superradiant neutrino emission is possible, which contradicts established no-go theorems.
method: The authors analyze the proposed mechanism, showing that pairing fermions into molecules does not eliminate the cancellation of interference terms due to fermionic anticommutators.
result: The cancellation persists, making superradiant neutrino emission impossible.
conclusion: The original proposal is invalid; the no-go theorem stands, and future work should respect fundamental quantum constraints.

title: Spectral Fusion For Identifying Early State Exclusion In Symmetric Quantum Spin Chains
authors: Mia Escobar, Valentin Garcia, Anastasiia Minenkova
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Perfect state transfer (PST) in one-dimensional quantum spin chains provides a natural setting in which quantum information transport can be analyzed using spectral methods. In the single-excitation subspace, the dynamics of a chain with nearest-neighbor interactions are governed by a Jacobi matrix, allowing questions of state transfer to be formulated in terms of eigenvalue distributions and symmetry properties of eigenvectors. In this work, we investigate the phenomenon of (ESE), whereby the overlap of the time-evolved state with the initial state vanishes at a time strictly earlier than the first occurrence of perfect state transfer. Building on earlier constructions of Hamiltonians exhibiting PST with and without ESE, we provide explicit Jacobi matrix realizations for arbitrary odd-length chains and establish general conditions under which ESE occurs or does not occur. We propose the process of (SF) to build infinite families of such Hamiltonians. These results broaden the known class of spin chains displaying early state exclusion and further clarify the role of spectral structure of the Hamiltonians.
tldr: This paper studies early state exclusion in quantum spin chains with perfect state transfer, using spectral methods and Jacobi matrices.
motivation: To understand and characterize early state exclusion (ESE) in symmetric quantum spin chains, which is a phenomenon where the overlap with the initial state vanishes before perfect state transfer occurs.
method: The authors construct explicit Jacobi matrix realizations for odd-length chains and derive conditions for ESE, using spectral fusion to build infinite families of Hamiltonians.
result: They provide general conditions for ESE occurrence and non-occurrence, and broaden the known class of spin chains exhibiting ESE.
conclusion: The results clarify the role of spectral structure in state transfer dynamics, but the direct relevance to quantum communication or information thermodynamics is limited.

title: Photon Shot-noise-limited Rydberg-EIT Electrometry
authors: Gyeongmin Ju, Ye Jin Yu, Heewoo Kim, Hansol Jeong, Jinhyuk Bae, Changhoon Baek, Han Seb Moon
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg-atom electrometry is a core technique in the development of highly sensitive quantum electric-field sensors. Its sensitivity based on atom-photon interaction is typically limited by photon shot-noise (PSN) and spectral broadenings. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a near PSN-limited Rydberg electrometry from a 85Rb atomic vapor cell. By engineering atomic coherence through control of residual magnetic fields and laser frequency noise, we achieve the Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) with the narrow linewidth of 1.6 MHz, yielding an enhanced spectral slope for high-sensitivity Rydberg-EIT electrometry. Under optimized superheterodyne detection conditions, we obtain an electric-field sensitivity of 12.5(8) nV cm^-1 Hz^-1/2 at 37 GHz, in close agreement with the calculated PSN limit. These results provide direct experimental evidence of the high-sensitive quantum electrometry and establish a practical route toward quantum-noise-limited Rydberg electrometry.
tldr: This paper demonstrates near photon-shot-noise-limited Rydberg electrometry using EIT in a 85Rb vapor cell, achieving high sensitivity at 37 GHz.
motivation: To overcome sensitivity limitations in Rydberg-atom electric-field sensors caused by photon shot noise and spectral broadening.
method: Atomic coherence engineering via control of residual magnetic fields and laser frequency noise, combined with superheterodyne detection.
result: Achieved 1.6 MHz EIT linewidth and electric-field sensitivity of 12.5 nV cm^-1 Hz^-1/2, matching the calculated PSN limit.
conclusion: Provides experimental evidence for quantum-noise-limited Rydberg electrometry, paving the way for practical quantum sensors.

title: QPredSGG: Hybrid Quantum Predicate Learning For Long-Tailed Scene Graph Generation
authors: Prerana Ramkumar, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) requires relational reasoning over objects and their interactions, but performance is often limited by severe long-tail predicate imbalance. Classical SGG models frequently rely on dataset statistics, leading to biased predictions toward frequent relations rather than fine-grained semantic predicates. Although existing debiasing strategies improve mean recall, predicate classification in current frameworks still often depends on large classical decision modules with high parameter cost. This work introduces a hybrid quantum predicate classifier for SGG by replacing the classical predicate head in Causal Feature Enhancement Network (CFEN) with a Quantum Predicate Head (QP-Head) trained using weighted cross-entropy. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first studies to evaluate a hybrid quantum architecture for scene graph predicate classification on Visual Genome 150. We study the effect of qubit count, encoding strategy, entangling structure, and circuit depth on relational prediction. The best 4-qubit QP-Head uses Amplitude Embedding and Strongly Entangling Layers to compress 4096-dimensional pair features into a 16-dimensional quantum-compatible representation, corresponding to a 256[MATH] reduction. It achieves an mR@100 of 57.25%, compared with 41.1% for the classical CFEN reference, while using only 96 trainable quantum parameters. Scaling to 8 qubits maintains strong long-tail performance, reaching an mR@100 of 55.38% with 384 quantum parameters, while the depth analysis shows a trade-off between expressibility and runtime overhead. These results suggest that compact hybrid quantum predicate heads can support parameter-efficient long-tail relational classification in complex visual reasoning tasks.
tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum predicate classifier for scene graph generation to address long-tail predicate imbalance, achieving improved mean recall with fewer parameters.
motivation: Classical SGG models suffer from biased predictions due to long-tail predicate distributions and high parameter costs. The authors aim to leverage quantum computing for parameter-efficient relational classification.
method: They replace the classical predicate head in CFEN with a Quantum Predicate Head (QP-Head) using amplitude embedding and strongly entangling layers, trained with weighted cross-entropy. They experiment with qubit count, encoding, entanglement, and circuit depth.
result: The best 4-qubit QP-Head achieves mR@100 of 57.25% (vs 41.1% classical) with only 96 trainable parameters, and 8-qubit version reaches 55.38% with 384 parameters, showing trade-offs between expressibility and runtime.
conclusion: Compact hybrid quantum heads can support parameter-efficient long-tail relational classification, suggesting potential for quantum advantage in visual reasoning tasks.

title: Efficient Description Of Parametric Amplification Of Quantum Pulses
authors: Victor Rueskov Christiansen, Klaus M{\o}lmer, Emanuel Hubenschmid
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single quantum pulse undergoing parametric amplification feeds into at most two pulses in the output. In this work, we present an efficient, analytical method for finding the quantum state of these output modes. Our method applies the amplification to the vacuum rather than to the input state, and subsequently applies a transformed version of the operator that creates the input state from vacuum. Given the input and output pulse mode functions, the method is analytical, and therefore computationally very efficient, and it can be readily generalized to multiple non-vacuum input modes. We exemplify the method by computing the output quantum states resulting from the input of a coherent, a Schr\"odinger cat, and a single photon input quantum state. We further employ the method to obtain the quantum state in one of the two output modes heralded upon detection of vacuum in the other, least populated, mode.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient analytical method to compute the quantum state of output modes from parametric amplification of quantum pulses.
motivation: To overcome computational challenges in describing parametric amplification of quantum pulses, especially when multiple input modes are involved.
method: The method applies the amplification to the vacuum state and then transforms the operator that creates the input state from vacuum, using analytical calculations based on pulse mode functions.
result: The method yields analytical expressions for output states for coherent, Schrödinger cat, and single-photon inputs, and also computes heralded states conditioned on vacuum detection in one output mode.
conclusion: The approach is computationally efficient and generalizable to multiple non-vacuum input modes, offering a practical tool for quantum optics and information processing.

title: Geometric Scaling Limits Of Phase-only Control In Multimode Coherent Systems
authors: Harikumar K Chandrasekharan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Control of coherent waves is often restricted to phase-only actuation in multimode systems, yet the resulting physical limits remain poorly understood. Here, we show that restricting control to relative phases confines dynamics to a compact manifold whose geometry produces isolated stationary interference basins with robustness governed by local curvature. Imperfections act as smooth perturbations that soften basin structure without eliminating stationary states. This geometry imposes a universal scaling constraint: although the number of stationary states increases with system dimensionality, achievable localization contrast degrades through leakage into uncontrolled degrees of freedom. Experimentally, we demonstrate this in a telecom-wavelength multimode photonic lantern, where coarse phase-only scans directly map stable interference basins, reveal efficiency-stability trade-offs, and identify robust operating regimes without transmission-matrix reconstruction, adaptive optimization, or system inversion. The framework establishes a practical calibration-free approach for constrained multimode coherent control and applies broadly to optical, microwave, acoustic, and finite-dimensional quantum systems.
tldr: This paper studies geometric scaling limits of phase-only control in multimode coherent systems, revealing trade-offs between stationary states and localization contrast.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of phase-only control in multimode systems, which are common in optics and other wave systems.
method: Theoretical analysis using differential geometry and experimental demonstration in a telecom-wavelength multimode photonic lantern.
result: Phase-only control confines dynamics to a compact manifold with isolated stationary interference basins; localization contrast degrades with system dimensionality due to leakage.
conclusion: Provides a calibration-free framework for constrained multimode coherent control applicable to optical, microwave, acoustic, and quantum systems.

title: Graphical And Algebraic Methods For Boolean Factoring
authors: Priyanka Mukhopadhyay Simon Martiel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem of factoring Boolean polynomials has significant applications in both classical and quantum computing technology. In this paper we have developed novel algorithms for factoring both ESOP and SOP expressions. Our aim is to optimize the AND-count. The AND-count plays a key role in determining the number of AND and Toffoli gates required to implement a reversible function with classical and quantum circuits, respectively. The first type of algorithms that we develop, are graphical. We reduce the problem of Boolean factoring to covering a bipartite graph with bicliques, and so optimizing the number of bicliques required to cover the bipartite graph, leads to reduced number of factors, and hence AND-count. The second type of algorithm is algebraic, and is derived from multivariate Horner method. We have compared the performances of our algorithms with existing popular methods like EXORCISM-4 and EPOEM2, on random functions of up to 12 variables. We have observed that our multivariate Horner method is substantially faster, while our biclique-based method achieves the maximum AND-count reduction. In fact, compared to EXORCISM-4 our biclique based method achieves up to 5 times reduction in AND-count.
tldr: This paper presents graphical and algebraic algorithms for factoring Boolean polynomials to optimize AND-count, which is relevant to reversible and quantum circuit synthesis, but does not directly address the user's research interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Boolean factoring reduces the number of AND/Toffoli gates in reversible and quantum circuits, which is important for circuit optimization.
method: Two algorithms: a graphical method that reduces Boolean factoring to covering a bipartite graph with bicliques, and an algebraic method based on multivariate Horner's method.
result: The biclique-based method achieves up to 5× reduction in AND-count compared to EXORCISM-4, and the Horner method is substantially faster.
conclusion: The algorithms offer significant improvements in AND-count optimization for Boolean factoring, with potential applications in quantum circuit synthesis, but the paper does not address energy consumption or other topics in the user's interests.

title: Boson Models With Interactions Of Arbitrary Order
authors: P. van Isacker
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper considers quantal many-boson systems that are described by a rotationally invariant and boson-number conserving Hamiltonian. The properties of a generic model are studied which treats N bosons of p different kinds with non-zero angular momenta l_1,l_2,...,l_p, possibly augmented with a (number of) scalar s boson(s). The order k of the interaction between the bosons is arbitrary and closed formulas are given for matrix elements between N-boson states for any k if p=1 and p=2. A recursive procedure is defined for arbitrary k and p. With the expressions derived in the paper it is possible to express symbolically a Hamiltonian matrix element between N-boson states as a linear combination of k-body interaction matrix elements. More generally, the formulas allow the evaluation of matrix elements of tensor operators that are not necessarily scalar nor boson-number conserving. The numerical implementation of the formalism is discussed and illustrated with a few examples.
tldr: This paper develops a general formalism for computing matrix elements of arbitrary-order interactions in bosonic many-body systems with rotational symmetry.
motivation: To provide closed-form expressions and recursive procedures for evaluating Hamiltonian matrix elements in boson models with interactions of arbitrary order, which are useful for nuclear physics and other bosonic systems.
method: The authors derive analytic formulas for matrix elements of k-body interactions for p=1 and p=2 boson types, and a recursive procedure for general p, using angular momentum algebra and boson number conservation.
result: Closed-form expressions for matrix elements of arbitrary-order interactions are obtained for one- and two-component boson systems, and a recursive method is given for general multicomponent systems.
conclusion: The formalism enables symbolic evaluation of Hamiltonian matrix elements and can be extended to non-scalar and non-number-conserving operators, with potential applications in nuclear structure and other bosonic systems.

title: Out-of-time-order Correlators For Swanson Hamiltonian With Interaction Terms
authors: Marta Reboiro M. W. Almasri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we compute the out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) for canonical position and momentum operators across a hierarchy of non-Hermitian oscillator models: the exactly solvable Swanson Hamiltonian, its Kerr-nonlinear extension, and parametrically driven variants. By employing the biorthogonal formalism required for parity-time symmetric quantum mechanics, we evaluate OTOCs both at zero and finite temperature, distinguishing behavior in the unbroken (real-spectrum) and broken (complex-spectrum) phases. Our analysis reveals how integrability, nonlinearity, driving, and parity-time symmetry breaking shape the temporal growth of operator correlations -- providing a clear benchmark for OTOC dynamics in non-Hermitian quadratic and weakly anharmonic systems. We further characterize critical scaling of the OTOC near the exceptional point and discuss experimental perspectives for observing these effects in photonic, circuit-QED, and trapped-ion platforms.
tldr: This paper computes out-of-time-order correlators for non-Hermitian Swanson oscillator models, analyzing their behavior across PT-symmetric phases.
motivation: To understand how non-Hermiticity, nonlinearity, and driving affect operator growth and chaos in quantum systems, using OTOCs as a diagnostic.
method: Biorthogonal formalism for PT-symmetric quantum mechanics; exact and perturbative calculations of OTOCs for position and momentum operators at zero and finite temperature.
result: OTOC dynamics differ qualitatively between unbroken (real spectrum) and broken (complex spectrum) phases; critical scaling near exceptional points is characterized.
conclusion: Provides benchmarks for OTOC dynamics in non-Hermitian systems and suggests experimental platforms (photonic, circuit-QED, trapped ions) for verification.

title: Quantum Circuit Partition As A Maze: Emerging Percolation Transition Via Path Finding
authors: P. Zentilini, M. Guatto, F. Preti, D. Arya, F. A. C\'ardenas-L\'opez, F. Motzoi, E. Prati
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum circuit optimization, circuit partitioning enables the optimization process to be parallelized across multiple devices. Each device is responsible for either reducing the number of selected gates or simplifying the local circuit structure. Most existing approaches to circuit partitioning are quantum-distribution-oriented and rely on splitting CNOT gates by introducing mid-circuit measurements and qubit resets. Currently, there is no criterion to determine how a circuit can be optimally partitioned without removing the CNOT gates for circuit optimization purposes. To address this challenge, we formalize the partition problem as a cutting path through a maze, where the CNOT gates represent the walls. We show that the existence of such a path separates quantum circuits into two classes through a percolation phase transition. In particular, it distinguishes a partitionable regime from a nonpartitionable one, arising from qubit permutations. Such permutations are generated by simulated annealing. We analyze its effect on the CNOT cluster from the perspective of network science and distribution analysis. Our results show that partitioning into two CNOT clusters is possible when the number of CNOTs is almost equal to the number of qubits. Based on this observation, we provide a scalable and practical criterion for identifying whether such a partition exists. Overall, our framework provides theoretical and numerical insight into circuit partitioning within quantum circuit optimization, forming the basis for algorithmic development.
tldr: The paper models quantum circuit partitioning as a maze-cutting problem and identifies a percolation phase transition that separates partitionable from non-partitionable circuits based on CNOT gate density.
motivation: Existing circuit partitioning methods rely on splitting CNOT gates, but there is no criterion to determine optimal partitioning without removing CNOT gates. This work aims to provide such a criterion.
method: The partition problem is formalized as finding a cutting path through a maze where CNOT gates are walls. Simulated annealing generates qubit permutations to analyze the effect on CNOT clusters, and network science and distribution analysis are used to study the percolation transition.
result: A percolation phase transition exists that distinguishes partitionable from non-partitionable circuits. Partitioning into two CNOT clusters is possible when the number of CNOTs is almost equal to the number of qubits.
conclusion: The framework provides a scalable criterion for identifying partitionable circuits, forming a basis for algorithmic development in quantum circuit optimization.

title: Essential Unitarity For Higher-Order Quantum Computation
authors: Radha Jagadeesan Samson Abramsky
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a semantic framework for higher-order quantum computation based on a boundary-centric presentation of compact closed categories, building on Kelly--Laplaza and Abramsky.Morphisms are polarized boundary linkings composed by execution, with a unit-free monoidal sum providing reversible control and branching. We identify a notion of generalizing unitarity from first-order processes to higher-order interfaces;at first order it coincides with standard unitarity, and at higher order it characterizes when information is preserved relative tothe boundary. Essential unitarity is the unique predicate compatible with dagger-monoidal structure, coherence reindexing, and currying, and reducing to ordinary unitarity at first order. Every morphism of the quantum core is essentially unitary. The framework realizes the coherent quantum switch and other one-slot, equal-ratio, purity-preserving supermaps as coherent pure-comb dilations. Extended Abstract appears in QPL 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a semantic framework for higher-order quantum computation based on compact closed categories and introduces 'essential unitarity' as a generalization of unitarity to higher-order processes.
motivation: To provide a rigorous categorical semantics for higher-order quantum computation that preserves unitarity at all orders, enabling the description of quantum supermaps and coherent control.
method: Uses category theory, specifically compact closed categories with a boundary-centric presentation, and defines essential unitarity as a predicate compatible with dagger-monoidal structure, coherence reindexing, and currying.
result: Essential unitarity coincides with standard unitarity at first order and characterizes information preservation at higher orders; every morphism in the quantum core is essentially unitary, and the framework realizes the coherent quantum switch as a pure-comb dilation.
conclusion: The framework provides a foundation for higher-order quantum computation with reversible control, with potential applications in quantum programming languages and the study of quantum supermaps.

title: Better Pauli Channel Learning With Maximum Likelihood Estimation
authors: Daniel Belkin, Faisal Alam, Matthew Thibodeau, Alireza Seif, Ewout van Den Berg, Bryan K. Clark
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Error mitigation in a noisy quantum device requires a very good estimate of the noise channel. The accuracy of probabilistic error cancellation is often limited by the high sample complexity of channel tomography. In principle, optimal sample complexity is attained by maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), but MLE is computationally challenging. We show that MLE can be made computationally tractable in certain cases of interest. For the common case of a 1D-local sparse Pauli-Lindblad channel, the likelihood function reduces to an efficiently-evaluable Bayesian network. We show that the resulting computation leads to substantially improved tomography. In addition, we demonstrate by simulation that this can lead to meaningful improvements to the overhead of error mitigation. We also discuss possible extensions of our algorithm to more general settings, such as non-1D circuits and non-Pauli errors.
tldr: This paper develops a computationally tractable maximum likelihood estimation method for learning Pauli-Lindblad noise channels in 1D-local sparse settings, improving error mitigation.
motivation: Probabilistic error cancellation requires accurate noise channel estimates, but channel tomography has high sample complexity and maximum likelihood estimation is computationally challenging.
method: The authors show that for 1D-local sparse Pauli-Lindblad channels, the likelihood function reduces to an efficiently evaluable Bayesian network, enabling tractable MLE.
result: The proposed MLE approach yields substantially improved tomography and reduces the overhead of error mitigation in simulations.
conclusion: The method can be extended to non-1D circuits and non-Pauli errors, potentially improving error mitigation in near-term quantum devices.

title: An Elementary Perspective On The Dirac Equation And Its Closest Relatives
authors: Rainer Picard, Sascha Trostorff, Marcus Waurick
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the Dirac equation in a real setting to show its close relationship to Maxwell's equation. In addition to analysing the classical Dirac mass term, we also inspect the alternative Majorana mass term and discuss their quaternionic structure and its consequences.
tldr: The paper explores the Dirac equation in a real setting, highlighting its structural similarity to Maxwell's equations and comparing Dirac and Majorana mass terms via quaternionic algebra.
motivation: To clarify the mathematical relationship between the Dirac equation and Maxwell's equations, and to analyze the quaternionic structure of Dirac and Majorana mass terms.
method: The authors reformulate the Dirac equation in a real (non-complex) setting and use quaternionic algebra to compare it with Maxwell's equations, examining both Dirac and Majorana mass terms.
result: The Dirac equation can be expressed in a form closely resembling Maxwell's equations, and the Majorana mass term exhibits a distinct quaternionic structure with implications for charge conjugation.
conclusion: The work provides a pedagogical perspective on the Dirac equation's structure, but does not directly address information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Quantum Information Harvesting With The Parallel Quantum Flow Algorithm
authors: Nicholas P. Bauman, Ajay Panyala, Chenxu Liu, Muqing Zheng, Meng Wang, Karol Kowalski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Quantum Flow (QFlow) algorithm provides a resource-efficient framework for describing correlated many-body systems on hybrid quantum-classical architectures. By enabling parallel utilization of quantum and classical resources, QFlow offers a scalable pathway toward simulations of realistic systems. In this Letter, we report a high-performance computing (HPC) implementation of the QFlow formalism based on a singles-and-doubles model. We demonstrate its performance for target spaces comprising 82 and 114 orbitals, where the flow includes all 6 active electrons in 6 active orbitals type active spaces. In the largest QFlow simulations, we optimize 1.17 million wave function parameters using the equivalent of 12 qubits. Despite the modest qubit requirements of the underlying active-space problems, the method recovers over [MATH] of the total correlation energy obtained with the coupled cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) approach for systems dominated by dynamical correlation effects, which remain challenging for existing quantum algorithms. We further show that the QFlow formalism retains high accuracy in extended basis sets with diffuse functions, highlighting its potential for realistic large-scale quantum chemistry simulations.
tldr: The paper presents a high-performance computing implementation of the Quantum Flow algorithm for quantum chemistry simulations, achieving high accuracy with modest qubit requirements.
motivation: To develop resource-efficient quantum-classical algorithms for correlated many-body systems that can scale to realistic chemical simulations.
method: The QFlow algorithm is implemented on HPC using a singles-and-doubles model, parallelizing quantum and classical resources, and tested on active spaces with up to 114 orbitals and 12 qubits.
result: The method recovers most of the correlation energy from CCSD for systems dominated by dynamical correlation, even with extended basis sets, while using only 12 qubits.
conclusion: QFlow shows promise for large-scale quantum chemistry on near-term quantum devices, but the paper focuses on computational chemistry rather than the user's research interests.

title: Mid-infrared Photon Counting And Resolving Via Efficient Frequency Upconversion
authors: Kun Huang, Yinqi Wang, Jianan Fang, Weiyan Kang, Ying Sun, Heping Zeng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical detectors with single-photon sensitivity and large dynamic range would facilitate a variety of applications. Especially, the capability of extending operation wavelengths into the mid-infrared region is highly attractive. Here we implement a mid-infrared frequency upconversion detector for counting and resolving photons at 3 [MATH]m. Thanks to the spectro-temporal engineering of the involved optical fields, the mid-infrared photons could be spectrally translated into the visible band with a conversion efficiency of 80\%. In combination with a silicon avalanche photodiode, we obtained unprecedented performances with a high overall detection efficiency of 37\% and a low noise equivalent power of 1.8[MATH]10[MATH] W/Hz[MATH]. Furthermore, photon-number-resolving detection at mid-infrared wavelengths was demonstrated, for the first time to our knowledge, with a multi-pixel photon counter. The implemented upconversion detector exhibited a maximal resolving photon number up to 9 with a noise probability per pulse of 0.14\% at the peak detection efficiency. The achieved photon counting and resolving performance might open up new possibilities in trace molecule spectroscopy, sensitive biochemical sensing, and free-space communications, among others.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a mid-infrared frequency upconversion detector with high efficiency and photon-number-resolving capability.
motivation: To achieve single-photon sensitivity and photon-number resolution in the mid-infrared region for applications in spectroscopy, sensing, and communications.
method: Spectro-temporal engineering of optical fields to upconvert mid-infrared photons to visible band with 80% efficiency, then detected by silicon avalanche photodiode or multi-pixel photon counter.
result: Overall detection efficiency of 37%, noise equivalent power of 1.8×10^-16 W/Hz^1/2, and photon-number resolution up to 9 with 0.14% noise probability per pulse.
conclusion: The upconversion detector enables mid-infrared photon counting and resolving, potentially advancing trace molecule spectroscopy, biochemical sensing, and free-space communications.

title: Optimizing The Sensitivity-Noise Trade-off In Non-Hermitian Sensing Via Off-Exceptional-Deficiency Operation
authors: Bin Guo Shangxuan Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central challenge in non-Hermitian sensing is that spectral singularities simultaneously amplify both the signal and environmental noise. We address this predicament in a double-chain Hatano-Nelson model featuring unidirectional interlayer coupling. At the exceptional deficiency (ED) limit, the system exhibits a macroscopically degenerate complex spectrum and a pronounced non-Hermitian skin effect (NHSE), yielding a sensitivity that scales exponentially with lattice size [MATH] while remaining robust across a six-order-of-magnitude detuning range. By introducing diagonal spatial disorder, we demonstrate that the NHSE is progressively suppressed, whith eigenspace cosine similarity analysis quantifying a well-defined fault-tolerance threshold. To reconcile the sensitivity-noise trade-off, we delineate "At-ED" and "Off-ED" operating regimes. While the At-ED configuration imposes fractional-order noise amplification (SNR [MATH]) that saturates at a suboptimal plateau, migrating to the Off-ED regime eliminates this geometric singularity and restores a linear scaling law (SNR [MATH]), achieving an SNR enhancement of several orders of magnitude. Crucially, this improvement is achieved while fully preserving the exponential sensitivity scaling, albeit at a slightly reduced absolute sensitivity compared to the strict At-ED limit. Our findings establish the Off-ED framework as a concrete paradigm for next-generation topological sensors that reconcile extreme sensitivity with robust noise immunity.
tldr: This paper proposes an Off-Exceptional-Deficiency operating regime in a non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model to resolve the sensitivity-noise trade-off, achieving exponential sensitivity with linear noise scaling.
motivation: Non-Hermitian sensing faces a fundamental trade-off where spectral singularities amplify both signal and noise, limiting practical performance.
method: The authors study a double-chain Hatano-Nelson model with unidirectional interlayer coupling, analyze the exceptional deficiency (ED) limit, and introduce diagonal disorder to suppress the non-Hermitian skin effect. They compare At-ED and Off-ED regimes using eigenspace cosine similarity and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scaling.
result: At-ED yields fractional-order noise amplification (SNR ~ N^{1/2}) saturating at a suboptimal plateau, while Off-ED restores linear SNR scaling (SNR ~ N) while preserving exponential sensitivity, albeit with slightly reduced absolute sensitivity.
conclusion: The Off-ED framework provides a concrete paradigm for topological sensors that combine extreme sensitivity with robust noise immunity, potentially impacting next-generation sensing technologies.

title: Atom Interferometry With Transverse Optical Modes
authors: Ryan Husband, Ryan J. Thomas, Yosri Ben-A\"icha, Rhys H. Eagle, Jessica Eastman, John E. Debs, Patrick J. Everitt, Michael Larsen, Eric Imhof, Charles A. Sackett, John D. Close, Simon A. Haine, Samuel Legge
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate atom interferometry using the transverse phase profile of an optical mode. As proof-of-principle, we use the helical phase windings of Hypergeometric Gaussian beams for Ramsey interferometry with ensembles of ballistically-expanding cold Rb87 atoms, and we show that the interferometer can measure rotations induced by a motor with a sensitivity that scales linearly with orbital angular momentum and interferometer time. We characterize the thermal decoherence of the interferometer, deriving and experimentally confirming a closed-form expression for the spatially-varying interferometer visibility arising near the singularity of the helical phase winding, motivating the use of condensed atoms in ring-shaped traps.
tldr: This paper demonstrates atom interferometry using the transverse phase profile of optical modes, specifically Hypergeometric Gaussian beams, to measure rotations with sensitivity scaling with orbital angular momentum.
motivation: To explore a new type of atom interferometer that uses the transverse phase structure of light, potentially offering advantages for rotation sensing.
method: Experimental demonstration of Ramsey interferometry with cold Rb87 atoms using helical phase windings of Hypergeometric Gaussian beams, and characterization of thermal decoherence.
result: The interferometer can measure rotations with sensitivity scaling linearly with orbital angular momentum and interferometer time; a closed-form expression for spatially-varying visibility near the phase singularity was derived and confirmed.
conclusion: The work suggests using condensed atoms in ring-shaped traps to mitigate decoherence, but the paper is primarily experimental atom optics with no direct connection to the user's research interests.

title: Atlas-nn: Adaptive Transfer Learnable Symplectic-aware Neural Network For Long-Time Hamiltonian Dynamics
authors: Changhong Mou, Dinghua Xu, Xiyue Zuo, Keji Liu, Yeyu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modeling Hamiltonian systems over long temporal intervals remains a significant challenge due to intrinsic multiscale structures and rapid nonlinear transitions. While Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) incorporate geometric invariants to improve stability, they typically rely on a fixed, externally prescribed temporal structure. This lack of adaptability often leads to accumulated phase errors and degraded accuracy in systems with heterogeneous temporal scales. To address these limitations, we put forward the Adaptive Transfer Learnable Symplectic-aware Neural Network (ATLAS-NN). Our framework augments the HNN architecture with a learnable temporal scaling mechanism that parametrize a nonlinear mapping of time, automatically adapting to the system's intrinsic complexity. We propose a two-stage transfer learning strategy: the model is first trained on a short-time interval to identify the Hamiltonian structure and optimal temporal reparameterization; the learned scaling function is then frozen and transferred to an extended interval for fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on nonlinear oscillators and the chaotic H\'enon--Heiles system demonstrate that ATLAS-NN provides a more efficient alternative to standard HNNs and traditional symplectic integrators, yielding nearly an order of magnitude reduction in long-time prediction error.
tldr: ATLAS-NN improves long-time Hamiltonian dynamics prediction by learning a temporal scaling function and using transfer learning.
motivation: Standard Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) suffer from accumulated phase errors over long times due to fixed temporal structures, especially in systems with multiscale dynamics.
method: The authors augment HNN with a learnable temporal scaling mechanism that parameterizes a nonlinear mapping of time, and employ a two-stage transfer learning strategy: first train on short intervals to learn the Hamiltonian and scaling, then freeze scaling and fine-tune on longer intervals.
result: ATLAS-NN achieves nearly an order of magnitude reduction in long-time prediction error on nonlinear oscillators and the chaotic Hénon–Heiles system compared to standard HNNs and symplectic integrators.
conclusion: The adaptive temporal scaling and transfer learning approach provides a more efficient and accurate method for modeling Hamiltonian systems over long times, with potential applications in physics simulation and scientific machine learning.

title: Factorizing Binary Tensors Into Quantics Tensor Trains
authors: Matthias Heller Paul Haubenwallner
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The conversion of functions to quantics tensor trains is a well-established procedure and can either be done analytically or numerically. Numerical conversion schemes are based on singular value decompositions, where access to the full tensor is necessary, or on cross interpolations, which only depend on sampling a function. When dealing with large binary tensors, the first approach becomes prohibitively expensive while the second approach might fail to converge due to the non-smoothness of the data. In this work, we provide insight into how binary tensors, where the positions of the non-zero entries are defined by some Boolean function, can be converted into quantics tensor trains with a hybrid analytical-numerical approach utilizing the rank product. The proposed construction scheme nicely reproduces results from the literature and can be used for discrete convolutions, the construction of discrete wavelet transforms or slicing and assignment operations of multi-dimensional quantics tensor trains.
tldr: This paper presents a hybrid analytical-numerical method to convert binary tensors defined by Boolean functions into quantics tensor trains, enabling efficient representation and manipulation of large binary data.
motivation: Existing numerical conversion methods for quantics tensor trains either require full tensor access (expensive for large binary tensors) or rely on cross interpolation that may fail due to non-smoothness of binary data. The authors aim to provide an efficient alternative.
method: The proposed scheme uses a hybrid analytical-numerical approach that leverages the rank product to construct the quantics tensor train representation from the Boolean function defining the non-zero entries.
result: The method reproduces known results from the literature and can be applied to discrete convolutions, discrete wavelet transforms, and slicing/assignment operations of multi-dimensional quantics tensor trains.
conclusion: The work offers a practical tool for handling large binary tensors in tensor network representations, with potential applications in signal processing and data compression.

title: Extremely Slow Scaling Of Minimal Hamming Distance In Quantum Sampling Data
authors: P. S. Golubev, I. A. Iakovlev, V. V. Mazurenko
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum data can be obtained from a diverse range of sources, including direct measurements from noisy quantum processors, cold-atom simulators, and classical approximations such as variational neural-network states. However, our ability to characterize these systems is fundamentally limited, as the available measurement data is often sparse compared to the exponentially large Hilbert space of the system. To address this, we propose using the average minimal Hamming distance calculated for a set of unique bitstrings as a robust metric revealing a universal power-law behaviour. Through various examples of real experiments and simulations, we show that the power-law parameters reliably capture the complexity of quantum states and identify quantum phase transitions from limited quantum information, without the need for accumulating extensive statistics or explicitly calculating physical observables.
