abstract: ArXiv:2606.04069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing privacy analyses for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) largely inherit assumptions from non-graph settings, overlooking structural correlations and stochastic training-graph sampling. In particular, node-dependent priors make type-I and type-II errors alone insufficient to characterize the best membership inference test. To address this, we introduce Bayesian Membership Privacy (BMP), a sampling-aware formulation of node-level membership privacy that incorporates node-dependent priors and treats graph sampling probabilities as part of the adversary's knowledge. BMP casts membership inference as a Bayesian hypothesis test and accordingly quantifies membership privacy in terms of posterior membership probability. We explore theoretical properties of BMP in relation to the existing definitions in the literature. We further propose a practical, sampling-aware auditing mechanism to estimate the parameters of BMP as a measure of node-level privacy leakage in GNNs. We conduct experiments on benchmark graph datasets and show that BMP yields fine-grained privacy insights that are not visible through global attack accuracy alone.
tldr: This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for quantifying node-level membership privacy in Graph Neural Networks, accounting for graph structure and sampling.
motivation: Existing privacy analyses for GNNs overlook structural correlations and stochastic training-graph sampling, making type-I/II errors insufficient for membership inference.
method: The authors propose Bayesian Membership Privacy (BMP), a sampling-aware formulation that treats graph sampling probabilities as adversary knowledge and casts membership inference as a Bayesian hypothesis test.
result: BMP provides fine-grained privacy insights not visible through global attack accuracy, demonstrated on benchmark graph datasets.
conclusion: BMP offers a more accurate privacy measure for GNNs, with implications for auditing and designing privacy-preserving graph learning.

title: Covert Influence Between Language Models
authors: Avidan Shah, Jay Chooi, Jinghua Ou, Shi Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As language models increasingly consume one another's outputs, covert influence -- a phenomenon where a sender's payload (the behavioral disposition it is conditioned to propagate) transfers to a receiver through carriers undetectable by humans -- becomes a growing risk. We characterize this risk across three interfaces: supervised fine-tuning, on-policy distillation, and in-context learning, and find that they vary in the scale of influence achievable without leaving behind human-visible traces. Using inference-time per-sample attribution scores, we study covert influence across all three interfaces with the ability to select carriers that amplify training-time influence, unlocking payload transfers that prior work could not achieve. We further provide evidence that covert influence with natural-language carriers is a distinct phenomenon from prior studies using number carriers, as the latter is more resistant to human detection and less portable across model families. Together, these results suggest that the risk surface for covert influence is broader than previously recognized, and we study pointwise attribution scoring methods as a tool to investigate and mitigate it.
tldr: This paper studies covert influence between language models, where a sender model's behavioral disposition transfers to a receiver model via natural-language carriers, without human-visible traces.
motivation: As language models increasingly consume each other's outputs, the risk of covert influence—where a sender's payload propagates undetected—becomes a growing concern. The authors aim to characterize this risk across different training interfaces.
method: The authors study covert influence across supervised fine-tuning, on-policy distillation, and in-context learning. They use inference-time per-sample attribution scores to select carriers that amplify training-time influence.
result: They find that the three interfaces vary in the scale of influence achievable without human-visible traces. Using attribution scores unlocks payload transfers not achieved in prior work. Covert influence with natural-language carriers is distinct from number carriers, being more resistant to detection and less portable across model families.
conclusion: The risk surface for covert influence is broader than previously recognized. Pointwise attribution scoring methods are proposed as a tool to investigate and mitigate this risk.

title: veriFIRE: An Industrial Case Study In Verifying Consistency Properties For A DNN-Based Wildfire Detection System
authors: Idan Refaeli, Maya Swisa, Itay Buchnik, Alon Zada, Guy Amir, Elad Mandelbaum, Ziv Freund, Guy Katz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present our ongoing work on the veriFIRE project: a collaboration between industry and academia, aimed at applying verification to increase the reliability of a real-world, safety-critical system. Specifically, we target an airborne platform for wildfire detection, which incorporates two deep neural networks. We present an end-to-end methodology for verifying in this system. Our approach encodes application-grounded requirements into solver-compatible queries for existing neural network verifiers. We study properties of interest over critical operational scenarios: (i) monotonicity of detector confidence as target intensity increases; and (ii) bounded detector response under physically plausible blur over the sensor. We instantiate these encodings using state-of-the-art neural network verification backends and evaluate them at scale on real background samples. For the first property, all verification queries are solved in under five minutes. For the second property, verification is substantially harder, highlighting key scalability challenges for richer, higher-dimensional specifications. Overall, the results demonstrate that meaningful, domain-specific guarantees can be obtained for industrial systems.
tldr: This paper presents an industrial case study on verifying consistency properties of a DNN-based wildfire detection system using neural network verification tools.
motivation: To increase reliability of a safety-critical airborne wildfire detection system by applying formal verification to deep neural networks.
method: The authors encode application-grounded requirements (monotonicity and bounded response under blur) into solver-compatible queries and use state-of-the-art neural network verifiers to check these properties on real background samples.
result: Monotonicity queries are solved quickly (under 5 minutes), while bounded response verification is much harder, highlighting scalability challenges for high-dimensional specifications.
conclusion: Domain-specific guarantees can be obtained for industrial DNN systems, but richer specifications require further scalability improvements.

title: Long-Term And Short-Term Transistor Aging In Deep Neural Networks: Impact And Mitigation
authors: Alireza Sarmadi, Virinchi Roy Surabhi, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Hussam Amrouch, Ramesh Karri, Farshad Khorrami
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are used in a variety of real-world applications including, for example, image classification and speech recognition. The inference accuracy of DNN implemented on hardware in integrated circuits (ICs) degrades under phenomena such as transistor aging. Aging slows down the switching speed of transistors, resulting in system-level timing violations due to unsustainable clocks. To maintain reliability for the entire projected lifetime, designers add guardbands to prevent timing violations; however, adding large timing guardbands causes losses in performance (speed or throughput). This chapter provides a detailed discussion of the effects of long-term and short-term transistor aging on DNN inference accuracy. Furthermore, to mitigate aging effects on DNN's accuracy and keep them at bay, a methodology for aging-aware retraining is presented in order to generate a resilient DNN even when aggressive (i.e., smaller than required) guardbands are used. This improves the inference accuracy of the DNNs even in the presence of aging-induced degradation. These effects are discussed in this chapter along with mitigation strategies on a hardware implementation of a DNN for image classification on an off-the-shelf image dataset. The application of short-term aging as an excitation mechanism for the detection of hardware Trojans in integrated circuits is also briefly discussed.
tldr: This paper studies the impact of transistor aging on DNN inference accuracy and proposes aging-aware retraining to mitigate performance degradation.
motivation: Transistor aging in integrated circuits slows switching speeds, causing timing violations that degrade DNN accuracy; guardbands reduce performance, so better mitigation is needed.
method: The authors analyze long-term and short-term aging effects on DNN hardware implementations and develop an aging-aware retraining methodology to produce resilient DNNs under aggressive guardbands.
result: Aging-aware retraining improves inference accuracy even with smaller guardbands, and short-term aging is also explored for hardware Trojan detection.
conclusion: The work provides mitigation strategies for aging-induced DNN degradation, with potential applications in reliable hardware implementations and Trojan detection.

title: Learning To Cooperate With Emergent Reputation Via Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xinwei Song, Yizhe Huang, Dengji Zhao, Xue Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reputation, the aggregation of peer assessments diffused through social networks, is a pivotal mechanism for promoting cooperation in social dilemmas ubiquitous to distributed multi-agent systems comprising agents with limited perception and cognitive capabilities. Exploring efficient reputation systems, comprising reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies, is a long-standing challenge. Previous work assumes predefined reputation assessment rules or models reputation as an intrinsic reward to learn policies, compromising the methods' ability for generalization and adaptation. To address this, we propose a distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning method [MATH] ([MATH]eration with [MATH]mergent [MATH]eputation), which jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies entirely from environment rewards. Notably, leveraging the underlying mechanisms of reputation, we deliberately design the constituent modules of [MATH] and the data flows among them, overcoming the latency and noise in the feedback signal, caused by the deep entanglement between reputation and policy. Experiments on the donation game and the coin game in grid world environments demonstrate that [MATH] effectively adapts to various existing reputation systems and co-players. Furthermore, we observe the co-emergence of reputation norms and cooperation in self-play settings. These results hold robustly across diverse social network topologies, underscoring the generalizability and efficacy of our approach.
tldr: This paper proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning method for learning reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies to promote cooperation in social dilemmas.
motivation: Existing reputation systems rely on predefined rules or model reputation as intrinsic reward, limiting generalization and adaptation.
method: The authors propose a distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning method that jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies from environment rewards, with careful module design to handle feedback latency and noise.
result: The method adapts to various existing reputation systems and co-players, and shows co-emergence of reputation norms and cooperation in self-play across different social network topologies.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates generalizability and efficacy in promoting cooperation, with potential applications in distributed multi-agent systems.

title: Bit-counting Complexity Classes
authors: Tayfun Pay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define a new family of complexity classes called bit-counting complexity classes, since membership depends not merely on the number of accepting paths, but also on the binary profile of that number. We study the relationship between this new family of complexity classes and the classical complexity classes. We prove that the classical complexity class [MATH] is contained in our comparison based bit-counting complexity classes [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH]. We further show that all of these complexity classes are Turing equivalent [MATH]. We also prove that classical complexity classes [MATH] and [MATH] are contained in both of our parity based bit-counting complexity classes [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: This paper introduces new complexity classes based on the binary representation of the number of accepting paths in nondeterministic computations, and relates them to classical classes like PP and ⊕P.
motivation: To explore a finer-grained classification of computational problems by considering the binary profile of accepting path counts, beyond just the count itself.
method: The paper defines bit-counting complexity classes (e.g., comparison-based and parity-based) and proves containment and equivalence relationships with classical complexity classes using standard techniques from computational complexity theory.
result: It shows that PP is contained in the comparison-based classes, and that PP and ⊕P are contained in the parity-based classes; also proves Turing equivalence among the new classes.
conclusion: The work extends the landscape of complexity classes, but its direct relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is minimal.

title: What If Prompt Injection Never Left? Exploring Cross-Session Stored Prompt Injection In Agentic Systems
authors: Yuanbo Xie, Tianyun Liu, Yingjie Zhang, Suchen Liu, Yulin Li, Liya Su, Tingwen Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern agentic systems transform LLMs from session-bounded assistants into stateful systems that persist and evolve shared world state across sessions through memories, filesystems, tools, and other long-lived contextual artifacts. This shift fundamentally expands the attack surface of prompt injection. However, prior works on prompt injection have largely focused on model-level threats within a single session, overlooking how cross-session persistent system state fundamentally changes the system-level risk of agentic systems. Inspired by stored cross-site scripting in web systems, we introduce cross-session stored prompt injection, where a successful injection can persist within agentic system state and silently influence future executions long after the original attacker interaction has ended. To systematically study this threat, we formalize stored prompt injection and develop a taxonomy of how adversarial content persists and affects agentic systems across sessions. We further develop a benchmark and sandbox toolkit to evaluate the risks of stored prompt injection, enabling quantitative analysis of attack success across different models, attack goals, and persistence channels. Our findings highlight that persistence transforms prompt injection from an ephemeral model-level threat into a long-lived system-level vulnerability embedded within agent execution state. We hope this work draws broader attention to this emerging threat and motivates the community to systematically study and mitigate system risks arising from persistence in agentic systems.
tldr: This paper introduces cross-session stored prompt injection in agentic LLM systems, a security vulnerability where injected prompts persist across sessions.
motivation: To address the overlooked security risk of persistent prompt injection in stateful agentic systems, inspired by stored cross-site scripting in web systems.
method: The authors formalize stored prompt injection, develop a taxonomy of persistence channels, and create a benchmark and sandbox toolkit for quantitative evaluation.
result: Persistence transforms prompt injection from an ephemeral model-level threat into a long-lived system-level vulnerability embedded in agent execution state.
conclusion: The work highlights the need for systematic study and mitigation of system risks arising from persistence in agentic systems.

title: Token Rankings Are Unforgeable Language Model Signatures
authors: Matthew Finlayson, Andreas Grivas, Xiang Ren, Swabha Swayamdipta
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model parameters are known to impose unique (to each model) geometric constraints on their logit outputs, which serves as a signature that identifies the model, but also leaks the model's final layer parameters when an API distributes logits. We investigate more restrictive APIs that expose token rankings (i.e., their ordering by probability, but not the probability values) and find that rankings also constitute a signature: every model has a unique set of feasible top-[MATH] rankings for sufficiently large [MATH]. Furthermore, the ranking signature is the first known (polynomially) unforgeable signature, since finding a model with the same set of feasible rankings is NP-hard. On the security front, we find that token rankings are already sufficient to approximately steal the final layer of the model, similar to logits, though the approximation is too coarse to forge the signature, and can be effectively countered by restricting the API to top-[MATH] tokens with sufficiently small [MATH]. Since the top-[MATH] required to present the model signature is generally smaller than the [MATH] required to prevent stealing, it is possible for an API to present an unforgeable signature without leaking model parameters.
tldr: This paper shows that token rankings from language models form an unforgeable signature that can identify the model and potentially leak parameters, but is not directly related to the user's research interests.
motivation: To investigate whether token rankings (ordering by probability) can serve as a model signature and whether they pose security risks similar to logits.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the uniqueness of feasible top-M rankings for each model and prove that finding a model with the same set of rankings is NP-hard, establishing unforgeability. They also empirically demonstrate approximate parameter stealing from rankings.
result: Token rankings constitute a unique, unforgeable signature for each language model, and can be used to approximately steal final layer parameters, but the approximation is too coarse to forge the signature.
conclusion: APIs can present an unforgeable signature by limiting top-M tokens to a small M, preventing parameter leakage while still providing a signature.

title: Global Sketch-Based Watermarking For Diffusion Language Models
authors: Daniel Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Watermarking methods for language models have been studied extensively in the autoregressive setting, where tokens are generated sequentially. These works largely focus on local-context schemes that perturb the next token's distribution as a function of its preceding tokens. In diffusion language models, distributions over many unresolved positions are jointly sampled, allowing additive statistics of the entire sequence to be tractable during generation. We propose a watermark for masked diffusion language models that controls a global, vector-valued sketch representation of the text. Compared to context-dependent watermarking, the sketch formulation decouples detection from the local contexts seen during generation, resulting in an order-agnostic statistic and a watermarking rule which does not manifest as a simple token bias. We analyze the distortion, soundness, and robustness properties of the method.
tldr: This paper proposes a global sketch-based watermarking method for diffusion language models, focusing on robustness and order-agnostic detection.
motivation: Existing watermarking methods for autoregressive models rely on local context, which is not suitable for diffusion models that generate tokens jointly. The authors aim to design a watermark that leverages the global structure of diffusion generation.
method: The method controls a vector-valued sketch representation of the entire text during the masked diffusion process, enabling additive statistics that are tractable. Detection is based on the sketch rather than local token biases.
result: The proposed watermark achieves distortion, soundness, and robustness properties, and is order-agnostic, meaning detection does not depend on the order of tokens.
conclusion: The sketch-based approach offers a new paradigm for watermarking in diffusion models, with potential applications in copyright protection and content provenance.

title: SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography (pqc) Implementation In Software Systems
authors: R. D. N. Shakya, C. P. Wijesiriwardana, S. M. Vidanagamachchi, Nalin A. G. Arachchilage
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is essential to protect software systems from emerging quantum-enabled threats. Although standardised PQC algorithms are now available, developers and organisations continue to face significant challenges in integrating them into real-world software systems. While existing studies primarily focus on cryptographic performance and algorithmic security, it provides limited understanding of the broader socio-technological factors that influence successful PQC implementation. This SoK investigates PQC implementation approaches and challenges through the Human, Organisation, and Technology (HOT) dimensions. By systematically synthesising existing approaches across these dimensions, we reveal a notable imbalance in the current body of knowledge, where technological solutions dominate, while human and organisational considerations remain underexplored. Our analysis further shows that PQC implementation challenges are not isolated to individual dimensions; rather, they emerge as interconnected socio-technological constraints that span HOT contexts, collectively shaping implementation outcomes. These findings indicate that PQC implementation extends beyond cryptographic replacement and represents a broader socio-technological transformation requiring coordinated approaches across all HOT dimensions. To address this gap, we propose the PQC-HOT model, a conceptual framework that explains how interactions among HOT dimensions collectively influence PQC implementation in software. The model synthesises the implementation interventions and challenges identified in the SoK into an integrated structure that supports systematic decision-making, planning, and organisational transition strategies. Based on these insights, we outline future research directions and design implications for scalable and sustainable PQC implementation in software systems.
tldr: This SoK paper surveys challenges and approaches for implementing post-quantum cryptography in software systems, focusing on human, organizational, and technological dimensions.
motivation: To understand the broader socio-technological factors influencing successful PQC implementation beyond just cryptographic performance and security.
method: Systematic synthesis of existing approaches across Human, Organization, and Technology (HOT) dimensions, leading to a conceptual framework (PQC-HOT model).
result: Identified an imbalance where technological solutions dominate while human and organizational considerations are underexplored; challenges are interconnected across HOT dimensions.
conclusion: PQC implementation is a socio-technological transformation requiring coordinated approaches; the PQC-HOT model supports systematic decision-making and planning.

title: Extending The El Farol Bar Game With Partial Observability And Incentive Design
authors: Iosif Polenakis, Kalliopi Kastampolidou, Theodore Andronikos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04753v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The El Farol Bar game is a classic model of coordination under uncertainty, traditionally treating the venue as a passive constraint. In this work, we re-conceptualize the problem by modeling the bar as a strategic player equipped with AI-driven learning capabilities. We extend the original framework to include partial observability, i.e., agents observe only subsets of past attendees, and transform the bar from a passive capacity threshold into an active mechanism designer that adjusts pricing policies to balance revenue, utilization, and sustainability constraints. Agents employ AI-based learning to form beliefs and adapt attendance strategies under incomplete information, while the bar uses policy learning to optimize dynamic pricing. The resulting two-sided learning system frames coordination as a co-evolutionary process between boundedly rational agents and an adaptive institution, offering insights into congestion management, resource allocation, and mechanism design in complex adaptive systems.
tldr: This paper extends the El Farol Bar game by introducing partial observability and AI-driven pricing, but it is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To model coordination in complex adaptive systems where both agents and institutions learn and adapt.
method: The bar is modeled as a strategic player using policy learning to set dynamic prices, while agents use AI-based learning under partial observability.
result: The two-sided learning system frames coordination as a co-evolutionary process between agents and an adaptive institution.
conclusion: The work offers insights into congestion management and mechanism design, but no quantum or thermodynamic implications.

title: The Usefulness Gap In Proof-of-Useful-Work: An Empirical Study Of Pearl's cuPOW Protocol
authors: Abhinaba Basu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pearl, a Layer-1 blockchain with high-profile AI industry endorsements, markets its Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW) protocol as simultaneously securing the network and performing AI inference. We present the first systematic empirical measurement of a deployed PoUW system, finding that Pearl's 24 EH/s network -- representing approximately 320,000 GPU-equivalents consuming an estimated 112 MW -- produces zero useful AI computation. Budget GPU rental prices rose 38% and utilization surged from 57% to 94% following the mining software's public release, displacing legitimate research workloads. Our measurements span five dimensions: (1) network composition analysis of 8,012 workers shows all have inference-capable hardware, yet the dominant mining software contains no inference code; (2) the verification protocol accepts random matrices by design, confirmed by 44 pool-accepted shares from our open-source miner across NVIDIA, AMD, CPU, and Apple Silicon hardware; (3) statistical distribution checks are trivially defeated by adversarial Gaussian sampling; (4) mining is unprofitable at current PRL prices ($0.21) across all GPU tiers (-54% to -72% ROI); and (5) the mining computation is commodity integer arithmetic portable to any hardware platform, offering no vendor lock-in. These findings quantify the verifiability-usefulness tension identified theoretically by Leinweber et al., providing concrete measurements of its magnitude and economic consequences in a deployed system.
tldr: This paper empirically evaluates Pearl's Proof-of-Useful-Work blockchain protocol and finds that despite marketing claims, it produces zero useful AI computation, wastes energy, and displaces legitimate research workloads.
motivation: To provide the first systematic empirical measurement of a deployed Proof-of-Useful-Work system and quantify the verifiability-usefulness tension in practice.
method: The authors measured five dimensions: network composition analysis of 8,012 workers, verification protocol testing with an open-source miner, statistical distribution checks, profitability analysis, and computation portability assessment.
result: All workers have inference-capable hardware but the dominant mining software contains no inference code; the verification protocol accepts random matrices; statistical checks are trivially defeated; mining is unprofitable; and the computation is commodity integer arithmetic.
conclusion: The PoUW protocol fails to deliver useful computation, highlighting fundamental tensions in such systems and suggesting that current PoUW designs are ineffective.

title: Dist-fl: Enhancing Security For TEE-based Aggregation In Federated Learning
authors: Guanlong Wu, Ju Yang, Zhen Huang, Jianyu Niu, Guoxing Chen, Jianzong Wang, Yinqian Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs)-aided federated learning protocols emerge as promising solutions to counter server-side adversaries and ensure the trustworthiness of the server. In this paper, we dissect existing protocols and demonstrate that server-side adversaries can still manipulate client selection and replay aggregation to compromise system robustness and privacy, by exploiting TEE limitations, i.e., state rollback and I/O manipulation. To this end, we present DIST-FL, a distributed system of servers guarded by multiple TEEs forming an append-only ledger for privacy-preserved, robust FL aggregation. Specifically, DIST-FL ensures operation linearizability to thwart state rollback attacks and incorporates inputs from reliable servers to mitigate I/O manipulation threats. We implement DIST-FL and conduct evaluations in WAN settings. Experimental results demonstrate that DIST-FL can effectively counter the proposed attacks and match the single-TEE's performance while offering a 6x throughput boost over its counterparts, leveraging TEE's computational advantages.
tldr: DIST-FL enhances security for TEE-based federated learning aggregation by using multiple TEEs to form an append-only ledger, preventing state rollback and I/O manipulation attacks.
motivation: Existing TEE-aided federated learning protocols are vulnerable to server-side attacks exploiting TEE limitations like state rollback and I/O manipulation, compromising robustness and privacy.
method: The authors propose DIST-FL, a distributed system of servers guarded by multiple TEEs that form an append-only ledger, ensuring operation linearizability and incorporating inputs from reliable servers to mitigate attacks.
result: DIST-FL effectively counters state rollback and I/O manipulation attacks, matches single-TEE performance, and provides a 6x throughput boost over counterparts in WAN settings.
conclusion: DIST-FL demonstrates a practical approach to secure federated learning aggregation using multiple TEEs, with implications for privacy-preserving machine learning and distributed systems security.

title: ThermoPix: A High-Spatial-Resolution ElectronicPhotonic Temperature Sensor Array With Microsecond Row Readout
authors: Md Rahatul Islam Udoy, Dharanidhar Dang, Wantong Li, Sumeet Kumar Gupta, Suman Datta, Ahmedullah Aziz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents ThermoPix, a CMOS-compatible electronic-photonic architecture for high-spatial-resolution temperature sensing. The proposed system converts temperature-induced wavelength shifts in a photonic interferometric sensor into timing information that can be processed by CMOS circuitry. We use a valley photonic crystal Mach-Zehnder interferometer (VPCMZI) as the sensing element, whose temperature-dependent spectral response is detected using an integrated waveguide photodetector and translated into a time-varying photocurrent. A CMOS readout circuit employing a phase-transition-material device performs threshold detection and generates a timing signal corresponding to the temperature-dependent crossing event. Circuit-level simulations demonstrate a temperature sensitivity of 3.15 ns/K, a row readout time of 2 us, and a sensing power-delay product (PDP) of 0.152 fJ. The required optical power per photonic cell is 150 nW, enabling energy-efficient array operation without requiring cooling or special environmental arrangements. We also present alternative photonic layer architectures for optical power distribution across the array. In one approach, we use different tap ratios along the row, while the other uses identical tap ratios with bidirectional excitation. The resulting average photonic cell pitches are 23.26 um and 38.52 um, respectively. The proposed ThermoPix architecture therefore provides a scalable platform for integrated temperature sensing arrays that combine photonic sensing elements with CMOS-compatible timing-based readout.
tldr: ThermoPix is a CMOS-compatible electronic-photonic temperature sensor array with microsecond row readout, using a valley photonic crystal Mach-Zehnder interferometer and phase-transition-material threshold detection.
motivation: To achieve high-spatial-resolution temperature sensing with fast readout and low power consumption, suitable for integrated systems without cooling.
method: A photonic interferometric sensor (VPCMZI) converts temperature to wavelength shift, detected by a waveguide photodetector; a CMOS readout circuit with a phase-transition-material device generates timing signals.
result: Temperature sensitivity of 3.15 ns/K, row readout time of 2 µs, sensing PDP of 0.152 fJ, and optical power per cell of 150 nW; two optical distribution architectures yield pitches of 23.26 µm and 38.52 µm.
conclusion: The architecture provides a scalable platform for integrated temperature sensing arrays, but its relevance to quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems is minimal.

title: Fairness And Strategy-Proofness In Automated Market Makers
authors: Frank M. V. Feys
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: No deployed automated market maker lets its liquidity providers vote on the trading function. We show this is structural, not an oversight. On the weighted-product family with [MATH] assets, no aggregation rule is at once fair and strategy-proof. Arrovian fairness forces a unique form, the weighted Aitchison centroid, the weighted geometric mean of the providers' preferred pools. But fairness forces mean-type aggregation and strategy-proofness forces median-type, and the only rule that is both is a single-provider dictator. The obstruction is sharp: it vanishes at [MATH], where a fair strategy-proof rule exists. Under the Frongillo--Papireddygari--Waggoner equivalence, the centroid is Genest's logarithmic opinion pool, and the impossibility transfers to externally Bayesian pooling.
tldr: This paper proves an impossibility theorem for fair and strategy-proof aggregation of liquidity provider preferences in automated market makers.
motivation: To understand why no deployed automated market maker allows liquidity providers to vote on the trading function, and to explore the theoretical limits of fair and strategy-proof aggregation.
method: The authors use social choice theory, specifically Arrovian fairness and strategy-proofness axioms, applied to the weighted-product family of automated market makers with multiple assets.
result: They show that for more than two assets, no aggregation rule is both fair and strategy-proof unless it is a dictatorship; for two assets, a fair and strategy-proof rule exists.
conclusion: The impossibility is structural and transfers to externally Bayesian pooling, implying fundamental trade-offs in decentralized governance of automated market makers.

title: From Agent Traces To Trust: Evidence Tracing And Execution Provenance In Llm Agents
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jiaqi Zhang, Taotao Cai, Zirui Liu, Qingqiang Sun, Zequn Sun, Zhangkai Wu, Mingkai Zhang, Yanming Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly solve complex tasks by interacting with external tools, retrieval systems, memory modules, environments, and other agents. These capabilities expand agent autonomy, but also make agent behavior harder to verify, debug, and audit. Final-answer accuracy alone cannot explain how an output was produced, which evidence supported each claim, whether tool calls were justified, how memory influenced later decisions, or where execution failures originated. Evidence tracing and execution provenance address this gap by modeling how retrieved evidence, tool outputs, memory items, environment observations, intermediate claims, actions, and final answers are connected throughout agent execution. This survey provides a systematic review and conceptual framework for evidence tracing and execution provenance in LLM agents. We organize related work around a unified provenance perspective that connects retrieval grounding, claim support, tool-use safety, memory lineage, observability, debugging, audit, and recovery. We introduce a taxonomy covering trace sources, evidence and execution units, provenance relations, tracing granularity and timing, representation forms, and trust functions. We review key methodological directions, including provenance representation, evidence attribution, tool-use provenance, runtime guardrails, provenance-bearing memory, trace-based observability, and failure diagnosis. We also map existing benchmarks, datasets, and evaluation metrics to provenance-related capabilities, and discuss how evaluation can move from final-answer correctness toward process-level accountability. Finally, we outline open challenges, including unified trace schemas, claim-level and semantic provenance, provenance-aware safety mechanisms, realistic execution-trace benchmarks, recovery-oriented evaluation, and privacy-aware audit infrastructure.
tldr: This paper surveys evidence tracing and execution provenance for LLM agents, focusing on trust and accountability in agent outputs.
motivation: LLM agents are increasingly autonomous and complex, making it difficult to verify, debug, and audit their behavior. Final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for understanding how outputs are produced.
method: The authors conduct a systematic review and propose a conceptual framework with a taxonomy covering trace sources, evidence units, provenance relations, representation forms, and trust functions.
result: They organize existing work around a unified provenance perspective, review methodological directions (e.g., provenance representation, evidence attribution, tool-use provenance), and map benchmarks to provenance capabilities.
conclusion: The paper outlines open challenges such as unified trace schemas, semantic provenance, and privacy-aware audit, advocating for process-level accountability over final-answer correctness.

title: Competitive Instability In Judo: The Hidden Mechanism Within An AI-Driven Non-Linear Dynamics Framework
authors: Attilio Sacripanti
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents a unified nonlinear dynamical framework for understanding, modelling, and teaching competitive judo. The Tori Uke dyad is formalised as a constrained multi body system whose behaviour emerges from symmetry breaking,coupling dynamics and transitions between attractor basins.Two fundamental instability archetypes rotational collapse Uchi mata type and gravitational lever collapse Seoi otoshi,suwari version, are identified as the core pathways through which all throwing techniques evolve.A Functional Instability Index is introduced as a dimensionless order parameter integrating geometric, dynamic, and coupling related variables, enabling the quantification of critical transitions such as Kuzushi,Tsukuri and Kake.Fractional Brownian Motion models the global displacement of the dyad, linking tactical exploration to the persistence structure of the interaction. An AI based pipeline extracts instability signatures from high frequency competition video, providing objective measures such as finite-time Lyapunov exponents,attractor topology and coupling stiffness.Building on these principles, a three level teaching framework is proposed, shifting judo pedagogy from a technique centred to an instability centred approach.This study establishes the first theoretical foundations for a predictive science of judo performance and outlines future directions for empirical validation, athlete monitoring, injury risk modelling and cross sport applications. .
tldr: This paper applies nonlinear dynamics and AI to model competitive judo, focusing on instability mechanisms and teaching frameworks.
motivation: To develop a predictive science of judo performance by modeling the Tori-Uke dyad as a nonlinear dynamical system.
method: Formalizes judo techniques as symmetry-breaking and attractor transitions, introduces a Functional Instability Index, uses fractional Brownian motion for displacement, and employs AI to extract instability signatures from video.
result: Identifies two instability archetypes (rotational collapse and gravitational lever collapse) and proposes a three-level teaching framework centered on instability.
conclusion: Establishes theoretical foundations for predictive judo science, with future work on empirical validation, athlete monitoring, and cross-sport applications.

title: The Influence Of Volumetric Shrinkage On The Metal Solidification Process Under Localized Energy Deposition
authors: Daniil V. Panov, Oleg A. Rogozin, Oleg V. Vasilyev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate simulation of metal melting and solidification under localized energy deposition is crucial for the advancement of beam-based manufacturing technologies. This study presents an extended multiphysics model that addresses a critical limitation of prior approaches by incorporating volumetric changes from phase transitions and thermal expansion, in addition to capillary and thermocapillary effects. Validation against the benchmark problems -- including a one-dimensional Stefan problem, two-dimensional solidification with free surface, and axisymmetric laser melting -- demonstrates the high fidelity of the proposed model in describing melt-pool dynamics and free-surface evolution. The numerical implementation features a novel mass-correction algorithm that reduces the mass conservation error by several orders of magnitude, while a smoothed mushy-zone formulation in the enthalpy method mitigates the discretization artifacts in solid-liquid interface tracking. The results indicate that volumetric shrinkage plays an important role in surface topography formation during solidification.
tldr: This paper models metal solidification under localized energy deposition, focusing on volumetric shrinkage effects, with no connection to quantum information or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Accurate simulation of metal melting and solidification is needed for beam-based manufacturing, but prior models neglected volumetric changes from phase transitions.
method: An extended multiphysics model incorporating volumetric shrinkage, thermal expansion, capillary and thermocapillary effects, with a novel mass-correction algorithm and smoothed mushy-zone formulation.
result: Volumetric shrinkage significantly affects surface topography during solidification; the model reduces mass conservation error by orders of magnitude.
conclusion: The model improves fidelity for manufacturing simulations, but the work is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Discussion On The Physics Problem Of A Boat Crossing A River
authors: Kyle Kou Yuchang, Simon Meng Zimin, Paul Zhang Yixing
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study addresses the boat river-crossing problem under non-uniform flow velocities by constructing three models: constant flow (Model 1), linear distribution (Model 2), and even-power function distribution (Model 3, adjustable via parameter n ). By using the vector addition, combined with the solutions of calculus and differential equations, the analytical expression of the ship's spatial trajectory under a fixed heading angle relative to the water flow is derived. For the shortest-time control problem, the Lagrange multiplier method is introduced to construct a constrained optimization model, and the analytical solution of the optimal heading angle that satisfies the boundary condition of reaching the direct opposite bank is solved. The research results provide theoretical support for the path planning of inland ship intelligent navigation systems, and the proposed multi-model analysis framework can effectively simulate the complex flow velocity distribution scenarios of real rivers.
tldr: This paper solves the boat river-crossing problem with non-uniform flow using calculus and optimization, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To provide theoretical support for path planning of inland ship intelligent navigation systems by modeling complex river flow velocity distributions.
method: Constructs three flow models (constant, linear, even-power function) and uses vector addition, calculus, differential equations, and Lagrange multiplier optimization to derive trajectories and optimal heading angles.
result: Derived analytical expressions for ship trajectories under fixed heading and optimal heading angles for shortest-time crossing under boundary conditions.
conclusion: The multi-model framework can simulate real river scenarios and aid intelligent navigation, but the work is purely classical physics and engineering.

title: Confocal Subsurface Backscattering Microscopy For Optical Identification Of Nanoscale Threading Dislocations In SiC Substrates
authors: Russel Cruz Sevilla, Hsiu-Ming Hsu, Irwan Saleh Kurniawan, Ruth Jeane Soebroto, Hsiu-Ying Huang, Jia-Ren Wu, Chia-Shain Chuang, Chao-Ming Fu, Sheng-Hsiung Chang, Wen-Chung Li, Chi-Tsu Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High density threading dislocations in SiC wafers facilitate reverse leakage and degradation, yet commercial defect inspection systems based on surface profiling and PL dark-contrast miss nanoscale TDs because they lack resolvable surface signatures and band-edge PL is uniformly quenched by background dopants or compensating defects. Here, we develop confocal subsurface backscattering microscopy to nondestructively detect TDs, based on the synergy of confocal filtering induced dark field configuration and strain induced photoelastic mechanism. By simultaneously suppressing specular reflection while enhancing optical scattering from TD induced refractive index perturbation, CSBM enables high contrast, high resolution TD imaging. Moreover, TD types can be distinguished by their distinct photoelastic scattering patterns. Our work establishes a simple but effective optical approach for direct TD identification that is more tolerant of surface imperfections, providing a practical route toward industrial in line inspection.
tldr: This paper presents a confocal subsurface backscattering microscopy technique for detecting nanoscale threading dislocations in SiC substrates, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: High-density threading dislocations in SiC wafers cause device degradation, but existing inspection methods fail to detect nanoscale TDs. The research aims to develop a nondestructive optical method for TD identification.
method: The authors developed confocal subsurface backscattering microscopy (CSBM) that combines confocal filtering to suppress specular reflection and strain-induced photoelastic scattering to enhance contrast from TDs.
result: CSBM enables high-contrast, high-resolution imaging of TDs and can distinguish TD types based on photoelastic scattering patterns.
conclusion: CSBM provides a simple, effective optical approach for direct TD identification that is tolerant to surface imperfections, offering a practical route for industrial inline inspection.

title: Center And Derivations Of Generalized Weyl Algebras Over $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}.$
authors: Akaki Tikaradze Ruben Mamani-Velasco
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be either a classical generalized Weyl algebra (also known as a noncommutative deformation of type A Kleinian singularity) or the enveloping algebra [MATH] over [MATH] In this paper we compute the center and derivations of [MATH] More specifically, we show that the center of [MATH] is generated by the Casimir element over the ring of the Witt vectors (of length [MATH]) of its [MATH]-center. Our description of derivations of [MATH] implies that if the ground ring is a field [MATH] of characteristic [MATH] then the restriction homomorphism [MATH] from the first Hochschild cohomology of [MATH] to [MATH]-derivations of the center is an isomorphism.
tldr: This paper computes the center and derivations of generalized Weyl algebras over Z/p^nZ, focusing on algebraic structures unrelated to the user's research interests.
motivation: To understand the algebraic properties of generalized Weyl algebras over rings of integers modulo prime powers, which is a purely mathematical question.
method: Algebraic analysis using ring theory and homological algebra, specifically studying the center and derivations via the ring of Witt vectors and Hochschild cohomology.
result: The center is generated by the Casimir element over the Witt vectors of its p-center, and derivations are described, showing an isomorphism between first Hochschild cohomology and p-derivations of the center over a field of characteristic p.
conclusion: The results contribute to the structure theory of generalized Weyl algebras but have no direct application to quantum computing, thermodynamics, or quantum communication.

title: Primitive Inhomogeneous Approximation For Fixed Non-singular Frequencies
authors: Xueyin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a high-dimensional primitive inhomogeneous Diophantine approximation result for fixed non-singular simultaneous frequencies. The frequency class is explicit and has full Lebesgue measure.
tldr: This paper proves a high-dimensional primitive inhomogeneous Diophantine approximation result for a class of frequencies with full Lebesgue measure.
motivation: To extend Diophantine approximation theory to inhomogeneous settings with primitive conditions, which has applications in dynamical systems and number theory.
method: The author uses analytic number theory and measure-theoretic arguments to establish the approximation property for non-singular simultaneous frequencies.
result: A primitive inhomogeneous approximation result is proven for a set of frequencies that is explicit and of full Lebesgue measure.
conclusion: The work contributes to pure mathematics, specifically Diophantine approximation, with no direct implications for quantum information or condensed matter physics.

title: Arveson's Gauss-Bonnet-Chern Formula For Hilbert Modules In The Multiplier-Algebra Framework
authors: Wang Penghui, Zhang Ruoyu, Zhu Zeyou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The present paper continues Arveson's program on curvature, Euler characteristic, and Gauss-Bonnet-Chern type formulae for Hilbert modules. For regular unitarily invariant complete Nevanlinna--Pick spaces on the unit ball in \(^d\), we prove that Arveson's Gauss-Bonnet-Chern formula holds unconditionally over the full multiplier algebra. Together with the polynomial-ring case, this shows that the validity of the formula depends essentially on the coefficient algebra. We then solve Arveson's finite defect problem in the same framework by giving a sharp classification of finite defect submodules. This problem is natural in curvature theory, since both curvature and Euler characteristic are governed by the defect structure. Finally, using commutative-algebra methods, we apply this classification to unitary-equivalence rigidity for finite-codimensional submodules of vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert modules.
tldr: This paper extends Arveson's Gauss-Bonnet-Chern formula for Hilbert modules to the full multiplier algebra of regular unitarily invariant complete Nevanlinna-Pick spaces, and solves the finite defect problem with applications to unitary-equivalence rigidity.
motivation: To generalize Arveson's curvature and Euler characteristic results for Hilbert modules beyond the polynomial ring case, and to classify finite defect submodules.
method: Uses operator theory, functional analysis, and commutative algebra methods within the multiplier-algebra framework.
result: Proved the Gauss-Bonnet-Chern formula holds unconditionally over the full multiplier algebra for the specified spaces, and gave a sharp classification of finite defect submodules.
conclusion: The validity of the formula depends on the coefficient algebra; the classification yields rigidity results for submodules of vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert modules.

title: Uniqueness Results For Quasi-analytic Functions On Compact Lie Groups And Homogeneous Spaces
authors: Sanjib Pradhan Mithun Bhowmik
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we establish a quantitative uniqueness theorem for quasi-analytic functions defined on compact, connected Lie groups [MATH] and on homogeneous spaces [MATH], where [MATH] is any closed subgroup of [MATH]. Our result extends classical Logvinenko-Sereda-type theorems to the setting of quasi-analytic functions on compact Lie groups and their homogeneous spaces. We introduce the quasi-analytic class of functions using iterates of the Casimir operator on [MATH]. This construction is justified by establishing that every function in this class possesses the strong unique continuation property. In particular, our result extends a result of P. Chernoff (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc., 1975) to the framework of compact Lie groups and their homogeneous spaces.
tldr: This paper proves uniqueness theorems for quasi-analytic functions on compact Lie groups and homogeneous spaces, extending classical Logvinenko-Sereda-type results.
motivation: To generalize quantitative uniqueness results for quasi-analytic functions from Euclidean spaces to compact Lie groups and homogeneous spaces, building on Chernoff's work.
method: The authors define a quasi-analytic class using iterates of the Casimir operator and prove that functions in this class have the strong unique continuation property.
result: A quantitative uniqueness theorem is established for quasi-analytic functions on compact connected Lie groups and their homogeneous spaces.
conclusion: The work extends known results to a new setting, but its direct relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is minimal.

title: Quantitative Uniqueness Properties For Functions On Compact Quasi-analytic Manifolds
authors: Sanjib Pradhan Mithun Bhowmik
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we establish quantitative uniqueness results for a class of functions defined on a quasi-analytic compact manifold [MATH] without boundary. This function class is characterized by the iterates of a positive elliptic linear differential operator on [MATH] and, notably, encompasses all functions with a finite spectrum. By employing a relatively dense observable set, we extend classical Logvinenko-Sereda-type results to this quasi-analytic framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if these functions satisfy a doubling property, observability holds from any measurable set of positive measure. Our results generalise the propagation of smallness from finite sums of eigenfunctions to infinite sums with an appropriate energy-parameter decay, thereby extending recent findings by Kukavica-Li (Proc. Lond. Math. Soc., 2025) to the quasi-analytic setting.
tldr: This paper proves quantitative uniqueness and observability results for functions on compact quasi-analytic manifolds, extending Logvinenko-Sereda-type theorems to infinite sums of eigenfunctions with energy decay.
motivation: To generalize propagation of smallness results from finite sums of eigenfunctions to infinite sums in a quasi-analytic setting, building on recent work by Kukavica-Li.
method: The authors use a positive elliptic linear differential operator to characterize the function class and employ a relatively dense observable set, applying techniques from quasi-analytic function theory and spectral analysis.
result: They establish that if functions satisfy a doubling property, observability holds from any measurable set of positive measure, and they extend Logvinenko-Sereda-type results to the quasi-analytic framework.
conclusion: The results generalize known propagation of smallness results and may have implications for control theory and inverse problems, but are not directly applicable to the user's research interests.

title: A Bias-Corrected Weighted Logistic Model For Gene Regulatory Networks: Functional Equivalence With The Product-of-Logistics And Comparison With Weighted-Sum Formulations
authors: Ismail Belgacem
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a bias-corrected weighted-logistic (bcw) formulation for ODE models of gene regulatory networks. Each gene's regulatory function is a single sigmoid [MATH] of the signed weighted regulator sum [MATH], with a combinatorial bias [MATH] depending only on the in-degree [MATH] and the steepness [MATH]. We prove this is the unique single-sigmoid correction recovering the critical-point value [MATH] of the product-of-logistics model and sharing its canonical equilibrium [MATH] under self-consistency. The bcw system inherits global [MATH] well-posedness, an explicit Lipschitz bound, a positively invariant box, and strictly positive basal output. We derive an exact algebraic identity for the discrepancy [MATH] as a sum over proper non-empty regulator subsets; a slope ratio [MATH] at the critical point; a curvature mismatch breaking the symmetry [MATH] for [MATH]; a no-go result excluding global equivalence by any state-independent constant; and a mean-field reading of the bias as a zero-order log-sum-exp approximation. At a shared equilibrium the Jacobians satisfy [MATH] with [MATH], giving a stability dichotomy. In the contractive regime [MATH] both systems converge globally and exponentially to the shared equilibrium at rate [MATH]. A two-gene self-activating negative-feedback motif illustrates the theory: the bcw form undergoes Hopf bifurcation at [MATH] of the product threshold and sustains limit cycles where the product is linearly stable, with eigenvalue amplification factor [MATH].
tldr: This paper introduces a bias-corrected weighted logistic model for gene regulatory networks, focusing on mathematical equivalence and stability analysis, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To improve ODE models of gene regulatory networks by correcting biases in weighted-sum formulations to match product-of-logistics models.
method: The authors propose a bias-corrected weighted-logistic (bcw) model and prove its functional equivalence to the product-of-logistics model under certain conditions, using algebraic identities and stability analysis.
result: The bcw model uniquely recovers critical-point values and shares equilibrium properties with the product model, but exhibits a stability dichotomy and can sustain limit cycles where the product model is stable.
conclusion: The bcw model offers a mathematically tractable alternative for gene network modeling, with implications for understanding bifurcations and dynamics, but is unrelated to quantum systems.

title: Need To Know: Contextual-Integrity-Grounded Query Rewriting For Privacy-Conscious Llm Delegation
authors: Xinyue Huang, Xiaochun Cao, Wenyuan Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs become increasingly woven into everyday workflows, user queries sent to cloud hosted LLMs routinely mix task-essential content with task non-essential sensitive disclosures, yet type based PII redaction is context agnostic and may raise two issues: over disclosing untyped sensitive context and over removing answer bearing spans. We recast privacy preserving query rewriting under Contextual Integrity: a span should be forwarded only if it is necessary for the task. We introduce DelegateCI-Bench, the first task based Contextual Integrity benchmark for privacy-conscious delegation, comprising 3,167 samples that combine high quality synthetic data spanning 11 tasks and 20 task types, WildChat based real user queries, and a medical challenge set with dense sensitive information. Building on this benchmark, we propose a CI-guided reinforcement learning framework that converts essential and non-essential sensitive spans into verifiable optimization signals, and train a query rewriter to preserve task critical information while suppressing unnecessary sensitive disclosure. Experiments show that our learned rewriter achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff, achieving up to +10.1 average utility over on-device baselines.
tldr: This paper proposes a privacy-preserving query rewriting method for LLM delegation based on contextual integrity, but it is unrelated to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning for physical sciences.
motivation: User queries to cloud LLMs often contain sensitive information beyond standard PII, and existing context-agnostic redaction fails to balance privacy and utility.
method: The authors introduce DelegateCI-Bench, a benchmark for contextual integrity in task-based delegation, and train a query rewriter using CI-guided reinforcement learning to preserve task-critical information while suppressing unnecessary sensitive disclosures.
result: The learned rewriter achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff, with up to +10.1 average utility over on-device baselines.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the effectiveness of grounding privacy in contextual integrity for LLM delegation, but its focus is on NLP and privacy, not on the user's research interests.

title: Caught In The Act(ivation): Toward Pre-Output And Multi-Turn Detection Of Credential Exfiltration By Llm Agents
authors: Pratibha Revankar Kargi Chauhan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents often place sensitive credentials in the same context window as untrusted retrieved content, creating a direct path for indirect prompt injection to induce credential exfiltration. We study this failure mode through three complementary defenses. First, we ask whether activation probes can detect credential access before output tokens are emitted. Second, we construct honeytokens from format-specific character models and calibrate detection with split conformal prediction. Third, we treat multi-turn exfiltration as a cumulative information-flow problem and track an estimated leakage budget across conversation turns. In controlled experiments on open-weight models, activation features separate benign and credential-seeking prompts with high accuracy, including under held-out encoding transformations. In a small synthetic multi-turn suite, cumulative accounting detects attacks that per-turn detectors miss. These results are preliminary: the multi-turn benchmark is in-house and small, the activation method requires white-box access, and the information estimator provides a practical signal rather than a formal upper bound. Still, the results suggest that credential-exfiltration defenses should combine pre-output monitoring, calibrated canary detection, and temporal leakage accounting rather than relying only on text-level output filters.
tldr: This paper studies detection of credential exfiltration by LLM agents using activation probes, honeytokens, and cumulative leakage accounting, but is unrelated to the user's research interests.
motivation: LLM agents may leak credentials via indirect prompt injection; existing output filters are insufficient.
method: Activation probes detect credential access pre-output; honeytokens with conformal prediction; multi-turn cumulative information-flow tracking.
result: Activation features separate benign and credential-seeking prompts with high accuracy; cumulative accounting catches attacks missed by per-turn detectors.
conclusion: Combining pre-output monitoring, calibrated canary detection, and temporal leakage accounting improves defense, but results are preliminary and require white-box access.

title: TITAN-FedAnil+: Trust-Based Adaptive Blockchain Federated Learning For Resource-Constrained Intelligent Enterprises
authors: Muhammad Hadi, Muhammad Jahangir, Talha Shafique, Muhammad Khuram Shahzad
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as an effective paradigm for collaborative intelligence while preserving data privacy. However, data heterogeneity arising from non-IID distributions and decentralized security threats remain significant challenges, particularly in resource-constrained enterprise environments. This paper presents TITAN-FedAnil+, a Trust-Based Adaptive Network for blockchain-enabled federated learning in intelligent enterprises. The proposed framework introduces affinity propagation-based adaptive clustered aggregation to identify and filter malicious updates without requiring prior knowledge of the number of attackers. In addition, GPU-accelerated vectorization is employed to improve computational efficiency, while a signed state jump mechanism enables lightweight blockchain resynchronization. Experimental results demonstrate substantial reductions in memory overhead, achieving up to 81% savings across 50 communication rounds on constrained 8 GB edge devices compared with the baseline framework. The results indicate that TITAN-FedAnil+ effectively improves robustness, scalability, and resource efficiency for secure federated learning deployments in intelligent enterprise environments.
tldr: This paper proposes a blockchain-based federated learning framework for resource-constrained enterprise environments, focusing on security and efficiency.
motivation: To address data heterogeneity and security threats in federated learning for resource-constrained enterprises.
method: Uses affinity propagation-based adaptive clustered aggregation, GPU-accelerated vectorization, and a signed state jump mechanism for blockchain resynchronization.
result: Achieves up to 81% memory overhead reduction on 8 GB edge devices over 50 communication rounds compared to baseline.
conclusion: The framework improves robustness, scalability, and resource efficiency for secure federated learning in intelligent enterprises.

title: Randomized Separations In Black-box Tfnp
authors: Fedor Kiselev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the relationship between deterministic and randomized black-box reducibility between problems in TFNP. Our main contribution is a general technique that establishes equivalence between these reducibility types from specific TFNP problems to any TFNP problem. In particular, we show that this equivalence holds for reductions from complete problems in PPP, PPAD, PPA, and [MATH]-PPP. In turn, it strengthens all known black-box separations, originating from these classes, to randomized separations.
tldr: The paper studies deterministic vs. randomized black-box reducibility between TFNP problems, establishing equivalence for reductions from complete problems in several subclasses.
motivation: To understand the power of randomization in black-box reductions within TFNP, and to strengthen known separations to randomized settings.
method: Develops a general technique that shows equivalence between deterministic and randomized black-box reductions from specific TFNP problems (e.g., complete problems in PPP, PPAD, PPA) to any TFNP problem.
result: Establishes that for reductions from complete problems in these classes, deterministic and randomized black-box reducibility are equivalent, thereby strengthening all known black-box separations to randomized separations.
conclusion: The results provide a deeper understanding of the complexity landscape of TFNP under randomized reductions, with implications for black-box separations.

title: Description-Code Inconsistency In Real-world Mcp Servers: Measurement, Detection, And Security Implications
authors: Yutao Shi, Xiaohan Zhang, Xiangjing Zhang, Xihua Shen, Hui Ouyang, Huming Qiu, Mi Zhang, Min Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a critical standard empowering Large Language Models (LLMs) to utilize external tools. In this ecosystem, LLMs rely on natural language descriptions provided by MCP servers to select and execute functions. This interaction implicitly assumes that tool descriptions faithfully reflect their underlying implementations, while this assumption is not mandatorily verified in practice. As a result, MCP deployments may suffer from a problem named Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI), where a tool's description of its capabilities and security boundaries is not consistent with what the code actually does. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of DCI in real-world MCP servers. We formally define the problem and propose a comprehensive taxonomy spanning functionality inconsistencies and undeclared side effects. Guided by this taxonomy, we develop DCIChecker, an automated framework that combines structure-aware static analysis with the Direct-Reverse-Arbitration prompting method to cross-validate tool descriptions against actual code implementations. We apply this framework to a large-scale dataset comprising 19,200 description-code pairs extracted from 2,214 real-world MCP servers. Our measurement reveals that DCI is widespread, with 9.93% of these pairs exhibiting inconsistencies. We further demonstrate that DCI creates a critical defense blind spot, facilitating varied risks from operational failures to stealthy malicious behaviors. Finally, we propose mitigation strategies to enforce semantic consistency and enhance the reliability of the emerging agentic ecosystem.
tldr: This paper studies inconsistencies between natural language descriptions and actual code in MCP servers for LLMs, finding widespread issues and security risks.
motivation: To address the assumption that tool descriptions faithfully reflect implementations in MCP servers, which is not verified and can lead to security vulnerabilities.
method: The authors propose DCIChecker, combining structure-aware static analysis with a Direct-Reverse-Arbitration prompting method to cross-validate descriptions against code.
result: Analysis of 19,200 description-code pairs from 2,214 MCP servers found 9.93% exhibit inconsistencies, enabling operational failures and stealthy malicious behaviors.
conclusion: Mitigation strategies are needed to enforce semantic consistency and enhance reliability of agentic ecosystems.

title: Odyssey: Reestablishing Confidentiality In Confidential Blockchain Via Delegated Execution
authors: Ju Yang, Weili Wang, Jianyu Niu, Jianzong Wang, Yinqian Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confidential blockchains leveraging Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have garnered extensive attention for transaction confidentiality. In this paper, we first taxonomize two classes of attacks against confidential blockchains, i.e., execution-inference and execution-replay attacks, which exploit TEEs' long-lasting side-channel and state-continuity issues to compromise the confidentiality of existing consortium blockchains. Then, we present ODYSSEY, a confidential blockchain that efficiently mitigates these attacks. The core innovations of ODYSSEY are the following: (1) Its delegation model: clients delegate transaction execution to their designated trustees, while other participants synchronize only the execution results, which significantly reduces the attack surface while preserving confidentiality and system performance. (2) Two novel techniques to improve ODYSSEY's efficiency and security: location-aware concurrent execution and delegation failure handler. Finally, we develop a prototype of ODYSSEY on FISCO BCOS, an enterprise-grade consortium blockchain platform. We have conducted various experiments, and our evaluation results show that in a WAN environment with 3 nodes, ODYSSEY can achieve about 4k throughput while keeping latency as low as 0.4-0.5s.
tldr: ODYSSEY is a confidential blockchain system that uses delegated execution to mitigate side-channel and state-continuity attacks on TEEs.
motivation: Existing confidential blockchains using TEEs are vulnerable to execution-inference and execution-replay attacks that exploit side-channel and state-continuity issues.
method: The paper proposes a delegation model where clients delegate transaction execution to designated trustees, and introduces location-aware concurrent execution and a delegation failure handler to improve efficiency and security.
result: ODYSSEY achieves about 4k throughput with 0.4-0.5s latency in a WAN environment with 3 nodes, effectively mitigating the identified attacks.
conclusion: ODYSSEY demonstrates a practical approach to enhancing confidentiality in consortium blockchains, but its relevance to quantum computing or information thermodynamics is minimal.

title: Clif: Cross-layer Leo-isl Fingerprinting For Physical And Network Attack Detection In Dense Leo Constellations
authors: Varun Kohli, Arijit Bhattacharjee, Samar Shailendra, Biplab Sikdar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) mega-constellations such as Starlink by SpaceX and Kuiper by Amazon rely on optical Inter-Satellite Links (ISLs) for autonomous mesh routing to provide low-latency telecommunication, Internet of Things (IoT), and security services globally. As commercial operators and governments deploy increasingly dense constellations and form multi-operator peering coalitions, ISL integrity becomes critical to both commercial availability and national security. However, there is a lack of real-world data for LEO constellations and existing real-time security approaches focus strictly on physical layer security, leaving blind spots in the coverage of network-layer and composite attacks. In this paper, we present a cross-layer, lightweight behavioral fingerprinting framework that fuses onboard physical-layer measurements with network-layer data to detect anomalies at low computational overhead. We construct an orbital simulation covering the first shells of Starlink (1,584 satellites), Kuiper (1,156 satellites), and a joint multi-operator peering scenario (2,740 satellites), injecting ten attack types that span spoofing, traffic manipulation, and routing subversion at varying severity. We evaluate three unsupervised, per-satellite detectors among which our Mahalanobis-distance-based detector achieves 99.5% recall on Starlink, 99.4% on Kuiper, and 94.8\% on the multi-operator constellation, while maintaining False Positive Rates (FPR) below 0.7%. Our results demonstrate that cross-layer feature fusion is not only necessary for comprehensive security of LEO constellations but highly cost-effective for large-scale networks while fitting into the strict onboard energy budgets of resource-constrained satellites.
tldr: This paper proposes a cross-layer behavioral fingerprinting framework for detecting physical and network attacks in dense LEO satellite constellations using optical inter-satellite links.
motivation: Existing security approaches for LEO constellations focus only on physical layer security, leaving blind spots for network-layer and composite attacks. There is a lack of real-world data and lightweight detection methods suitable for resource-constrained satellites.
method: The authors construct orbital simulations of Starlink, Kuiper, and a joint multi-operator peering scenario, injecting ten attack types. They evaluate three unsupervised per-satellite detectors, with a Mahalanobis-distance-based detector performing best.
result: The Mahalanobis-distance-based detector achieves 99.5% recall on Starlink, 99.4% on Kuiper, and 94.8% on the multi-operator constellation, with false positive rates below 0.7%.
conclusion: Cross-layer feature fusion is necessary and cost-effective for comprehensive security of LEO constellations, fitting within the strict energy budgets of satellites.

title: Provably Auditable And Safe Llm Agents From Human-Authored Ontologies
authors: Aaron Sterling
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the LLM agent architecture Agentic Redux, intended for use with nontrivial problem domains that require linear auditability. Using the typed lambda calculus, we prove that, run on appropriate domains, Agentic Redux executions are semantically guaranteed to be correct, with all decisions recorded in an append-only ledger. We present two production-grade appropriate domains, in healthcare billing compliance, and security vulnerability disclosure. Working code for Agentic Redux run on both domains is available in a supporting code repository. We also introduce Ontology-First Agent Design, a methodology for creation of agent frameworks on a problem domain, in which a human expert ontologizes the problem domain with Basic Formal Ontology, and then assigns an LLM to derive roles that agents and humans-in-the-loop can fill, in order to work the problems in the domain.
tldr: This paper presents an LLM agent architecture with formal correctness guarantees using typed lambda calculus and ontologies, applied to healthcare and security domains.
motivation: To create LLM agents that are provably auditable and safe for high-stakes domains like healthcare billing and security vulnerability disclosure.
method: The authors introduce Agentic Redux, an architecture that uses typed lambda calculus to ensure semantic correctness and an append-only ledger for auditability, combined with Ontology-First Agent Design using Basic Formal Ontology.
result: The architecture is proven to guarantee correct executions on appropriate domains, with working code provided for two production-grade domains.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a methodology for building auditable LLM agents, but its relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is negligible.

title: $A$-Generalized Hessian pre-Lie Algebras And $A$-Generalized Yang--Baxter Equations
authors: Yining Sun, Zeyu Hao, Ziyi Zhang, Liangyun Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.04041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by the problem of constructing ([MATH]-)pre-Lie algebra structures on the dual space of a pre-Lie algebra, we introduce the \(A\)-generalized Yang--Baxter equation as a generalization of the Yang--Baxter equation of pre-Lie algebras. We study its symmetric solutions through \(A\)-generalized Hessian pre-Lie algebras and split these solutions into two types. We further consider factorizable solutions of this equation and establish a one-to-one correspondence between them and generalized quadratic Rota--Baxter pre-Lie algebras of nonzero weight.
